title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to Press
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to Press Remarks Marco Rubio, Secretary of State Barranquilla Marriott Hotel Barranquilla, Colombia September 8, 2026 SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) Ready? Ready. Are we going to do this in Spanish or English? In Spanglish. Let’s go. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Yes, in Spanish and English QUESTION: Spanglish. SECRETARY RUBIO: In Spanglish? QUESTION: Yeah. (Laughter.) QUESTION: Secretary Rubio, will the tariffs on Colombia be lifted by you [all] SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) We are working on that. Obviously, this is part of a legal process. It does not apply specifically to Colombia, [it applies] to every country in the world. After there was a Supreme Court decision that knocked down the system that the President had implemented, we had to start this process again. That is why we want to deal with this, there are active negotiations in progress at this time, and we expect that we will have a positive result for the United States and for Colombia as well. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Mr. Secretary, former President Gustavo Petro says that being added to the OFAC list was a mistake and he states it is unfair. Do you think he could be taken off (inaudible) from the OFAC list, are there any investigations currently underway against former President Petro? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) I am not going to discuss investigations. What I can say is that, obviously, all decisions taken at the OFAC level are fact-based, documents and evidence, and that was the determination made by the Treasury Department at that time. Aside from that, I cannot respond to the specific investigation. I also don’t have any announcements QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Secretary, we are live for Noticias Caracol (Caracol News)… SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) Live? Yes? Oh, I can’t make any mistakes. Go ahead. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) President de la Espriella has announced a strategic security plan. You said it yourself. Security and prosperity for the region. Regarding Shield of the Americas, what role will the United States play in relation to this request made by Colombia regarding military operations in our country? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) First, two things. Number one, the relationship between the United States and Colombia concerning security issues has been on-going for almost 20-plus years; they’re the strongest in the hemisphere. It was interrupted for a time, but not completely. Obviously, we want to hear more details about what the President’s ideas are regarding how we can cooperate, but we are willing to do everything necessary within the bounds of the law in Colombia, within the decisions made by its sovereign leaders. Obviously, we are willing to do a lot, everything possible between our two countries. As to the Shield, the Shield is important. The President has invited us to open an operations center in Medellin, for the entire region, not just Colombia. And I think that the capability that exists in Colombia’s security system is enormous, it’s incredible. That hasn’t gone away. Unfortunately, there were three or four years when they weren’t receiving the necessary resources. But the key function of any government, any country in the world, is security. It’s the most important thing any government does. And we are willing to work in any way possible, in anything that is asked of us; they have to ask. We are not going to dictate. But whatever is asked of us, and is made possible for us, we are willing to provide. If it is possible, if it is asked of us. Because of the importance Colombia has and because it has been our strongest ally in security matters, and economic as well, in the region for over two decades. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, did you speak with the president about tariffs at all? They had – Colombia had asked that the U.S. lift tariffs to help with the reconstruction. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. As I explained earlier, and I did — QUESTION: And did you say yes? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, hold on. But I answered this question in Spanish, so maybe I should have just answered in English. QUESTION: Ah, I (inaudible). SECRETARY RUBIO: Okay, well, you’ve got to – you’ve got to brush up on your Spanish. (Laughter.) QUESTION: Sorry. Yes, I should. SECRETARY RUBIO: Okay. But it’s going to be the same answer. As you know, the Supreme Court made that decision, and so the whole system the President had used for tariffs came down, so we had to – he had to reinstitute it all through the 301 process. It’s a very legalistic process. That said, I think the President has a desire – the President of the United States has a desire – to reach an agreement with Colombia as soon as possible. Ambassador Greer has been working with Colombian authorities on that negotiation. I think it’s going very well, and I hope to have good news soon in regards to that once such an agreement can be reached. But that is really the way around the 301, or the way the 302 – I’m sorry – investigations and the 302 process, is you have to reach an agreement and an accord on a bilateral basis. We are committed to doing that. Those talks are ongoing. They’ve already – I think there’s been two rounds of that discussion, and good progress is being made, but obviously no announcement today but hopefully soon. And President Trump desires to reach an agreement on that. QUESTION: Secretary, can you speak about the latest — QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Secretary of State, as part of the Shield of the Americas initiative, are there plans to build U.S. military bases in Colombia? And, my second question has to do with the anti-drug certification for Colombia. Has the United States considered restoring that certification to our country? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) Okay, the co-First, regarding the certification, obviously the cooperation this new government is demonstrating is different from the past, and that will be taken into account. That determination is made once a year. So, this year’s determination is based on activities that occurred last year. The new determination has to be made next year. But obviously, the cooperation is very different, and I think that will be reflected in the decision. In terms of the first point, about the bases, look, this is sovereign Colombian territory. We can open a military base; we have to be invited to do so. We have to study whether it’s feasible. In many cases, these bases are joint bases, which we have in common, as we have in other parts of the world. So, if that’s proposed, if that’s been discussed, it will have to be with the cooperation of the Colombian authorities, and they have to have requested it. And obviously, the U.S. Department of War also has to study whether it’s feasible, what the cost would be, and everything else. What is beyond doubt is that the United States will cooperate with the Colombian government with everything necessary to confront this regional threat, not just in Colombia. It is a regional threat that affects many countries in the region, including the United States. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) There has been talk about the border of Colombia and Venezuela- And it is a critical issue. President de la Espriella will discuss it now. Will the ELN, designated as a terrorist organization by the United States, be bombed on the border? Are there talks with Delcy Rodríguez? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) Well, without a doubt, that needs to be discussed, and it has been discussed in the past. It’s not sustainable to have drug trafficking, criminal, and terrorist organizations operating within the national territory of another country and threatening others within this country. They operate with impunity, and they have done so for a long time. I’ve spoken about this for a long time. This will undoubtedly be key to improving relations between Venezuela and Colombia because it’s a direct threat to Colombia. Imagine if a criminal gang were operating from one territory across the border, entering your country, committing crimes, murders, and attacks, and then returning and hiding in another country. That’s not sustainable. We have to confront it. Obviously, we want to do so in cooperation. And this has been discussed and will continue to be discussed, not only with the interim authorities now in Venezuela, but also with a future democratic government within Venezuela. Because this will take time to resolve, but, without a doubt, we have to confront this threat. This threat, as it exists now, cannot continue. A solution must be found, and it must be quickly. QUESTION: (inaudible) (In Spanish.) Officer Number Three, in the Odebrecht corruption case, President de la Espriella has requested that the name of Officer Number Three, which was revealed in court documents in the United States, be disclosed. Will the United States disclose who it is? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) I don’t know about that specific case. I can look into is and give you an answer. I know…that case, I have not been specifically told about that case. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Secretary, what will the cooperation of the United States with Colombia look like? What private investment will arrive? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) Those are two separate things… QUESTION: (In Spanish.) How to move from Plan Colombia to Plan Patriota (Patriot Plan) that the president requested? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) It’s the same question then. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Exactly SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) More or less. I will say. Obviously, that plan is being formulated right now. The President spoke openly and publicly today about different things: military purchases he wants to make, the radar system, the intelligence system, everything else. Which is necessary and we are willing and open to cooperate in that area. So, the Department of War is working very closely with the new administration on exactly what they’re asking for and how it can be provided. Beyond that, the good thing is that it already exists, there have been many relationships. That was suspended to some extent in recent years, but there’s more than 20 years of history of joint cooperation. I even mentioned that a few years ago, when I visited Honduras as a senator, I found that the trainers of the Honduran forces were Colombians, who had originally been trained by the United States. So that’s the level Colombia reached, being able not only to protect its own country but also to contribute to the training of police and military forces in other countries. So that relationship with the United States, at the security level, was never suspended, and many of the same people are still there. They just didn’t have the resources and emphasis in recent years. In terms of what we can specifically do, that’s being worked out at the Department of Defense level, our Department of War, with the Colombian authorities. They will say, “This is our strategy.” Obviously, these are the needs we have. And they will work together to determine what is specifically needed. What I can tell you is that President Trump is willing to provide everything possible to help Colombia confront this threat, which for three or four years that threat was not really confronted. QUESTION : (Spanish) It wouldn’t go through Congress in view of them having to approve it? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) Yes, but that already exists. For example, there are already funds within our annual budget for security in Colombia. Those funds are already there; what we’re discussing now is how those funds will be allocated, what specific needs they will address. And obviously, the President of Colombia already has very specific ideas, but there are other ideas we could potentially propose. In short, we are willing. President Trump has said so-he told me personally, he is willing to do everything possible to help Colombia confront this threat, because we see a government of people with the energy and interest to do so. QUESTION: Secretary, can you speak about the war in – with a lot of American public attention focused on the latest status of affairs in Iran, can you speak about the U.S. strikes on the Iranian tankers and explain — SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: — what the back-and-forth has been in the last 24 hours? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, the back-and-forth is pretty straightforward, and that is that Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers. And I think you’ll see that again today. QUESTION: Can you talk a little bit more – I know you already addressed this in Spanish, but for the English speakers here – about the security cooperation with Colombia? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: I mean, are the boat strikes going to continue? They don’t seem – or are there — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, those are tactical decisions. What I – here’s what I can say to you, and that is that the United States already has a longstanding and very deep security relationship with Colombia. Unfortunately, it was impeded over the last three or four years by political leadership here, but that has now changed. So our hope is not just to get back to what we used to do together, which was a lot, but perhaps to build upon it. And I think you have a president here now that’s very interested in making that happen. And so I know that there are ongoing talks directly engaged between the security forces here and the Department of War on exactly the kinds of things they want to cooperate on, the kinds of equipment they would like to purchase. In the end, the majority of this fight the Colombian authorities are willing to take on themselves. They just need our help with equipment; they need our help with intelligence; they need our help sometimes with some specialized training. But – and if I say “help,” I mean oftentimes that they want to purchase these things. So that’s a very active and vibrant conversation that’s going on right now, and I think we have a great foundation to build on because we have almost two decades of very close – the closest security cooperation in the entire hemisphere was between the U.S. and Colombia for almost two decades. So that’s an incredible foundation to build on. So I don’t think it will take long to get back to the levels we were at before, and in fact, potentially exceed it, again, based on what the Colombia authorities ask for. QUESTION: Could that be boots on – could that mean boots on the ground for American, U.S. troops? SECRETARY RUBIO: I don’t think that that’s what they’ve ever asked us for. The Colombians have never asked for American soldiers to come into Colombia and take on drug – they’ve asked for our help in training. They’ve asked for our help with intelligence and targeting and things of this nature in the past. They’ve asked for help with the specialized equipment. So I’ve never heard anyone suggest that to us. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Regarding the report that President Netanyahu knew about the attacks before October 7, will this in any way change the cooperation that the United States has provided him? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) I haven’t seen those reports, I’ve seen those rumors, but I’ve never seen that… QUESTION: (In Spanish) A report from the Haaretz newspaper, which published that the president. SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) Yes, but remember, Israel is having elections right now, and this whole election cycle is unfolding, and it depends on the newspaper. I can’t comment on something for which I have no evidence. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Now that the time has come for reconstruction after the earthquake, two issues arise: Is a reconstruction plan currently underway following this emergency? And on the other hand, regarding what the President just mentioned about migration, complying with several of the protocols you have implemented. Regarding reconstruction, have there been any specific announcements concerning investment, funding in this process? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) No, first, what they’re doing right now here is studying exactly what the needs are for housing, infrastructure, energy, and so on. And then what we want to see is how many American companies are willing to invest. Obviously, it won’t all be American companies, and there will certainly be Colombian companies that will participate, either as partners in those investments or primarily as the main source of aid. But, in short, we’re looking what the plan is. They’re presenting, preparing that very specific plan about exactly which reconstruction areas they want to focus on and how we can work on a source, a reconstruction fund, in which we can use different U.S. agencies to attract not just investment, but also professional companies from the United States, and possibly from other parts of the world as well. So that they can contribute to that effort in terms of work of reconstruction, cleanup work, everything that’s needed. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, what’s your read on the latest – what’s your read on the latest with Russia and Ukraine after the weekend talks and the President’s call with President Putin? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we had – look, there were – I think it was a good sort of a – there were substantive talks. I don’t want to characterize them as good or bad or productive or unproductive, other than they were substantive. New ideas were bandied about. It’s a very difficult conflict, one that we’ve seen why – for now an extended period of time you haven’t seen much movement on either side in terms of their willingness to make accommodations, and both sides have very bright red lines up to this point. But these were substantive talks over the weekend, both in Kyiv and in Moscow, and hopefully from that we can create a path forward to restart talks that the United States has always been willing to play the role of a mediator. So I don’t want to be overly optimistic, but I also am not pessimistic in the sense that I think there’s an opportunity over the next few weeks to develop a roadmap moving forward to restart talks and maybe reach a conclusion there that’s acceptable to both sides. Because that’s what it’s going to take in order for it to end; both sides will have to agree to it. So the way I would characterize this weekend was it was productive in the sense that it restarted engagement after months of not really being engaged in this, and from our end anyways, because we just didn’t see it progressing, and there were substantive ideas put on the table that for the first time at least there seemed to be some general openness to. But a lot of work remains. I don’t want to over-characterize. QUESTION: (Inaudible) (In Spanish.) The request for the consulate in Barranquilla. SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish) Well, that brought up to me for the first time today when I arrived at the airport. The first time it’s been brought up to me. So, we have to investigate it, and I’m not against it. It would be wonderful if we could do it, but obviously we have an internal process we have to go through. But that idea was presented to me three or four hours ago. So, give me a couple of days, or even a couple of weeks, to make that decision. But I certainly love being here. This is a city with a lot of energy, with a great history, very similar to Miami in terms of the climate and the environment. And yes, it’s logical, we want to do it. And obviously the fact that the President is here for so long. That he is here for so long also makes us think a bit about whether we should do it, because as he has said, he doesn’t simply want to be a president in Bogotá, he wants to be a president at the regional level, where Colombia lives, and specifically in the Caribbean area. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) We are live. There’s been talk about the possibility of a meeting between President Abelardo de la Espriella and President Donald Trump. And what is that priority? Or is your priority establishing a military base here? QUESTION: (In Spanish.) And why not in Barranquilla? SECRETARY RUBI: (In Spanish.) Well, I was asked about the military base, so as I said, that needs to be studied. And that also… that has to come through a permit from the Colombian government. There are still some steps to take. I’m not against it. It’s possible, but that’s something that hasn’t been discussed much up to this point, although the possibility is being studied. If it’s not a military base, it’s a joint base, or a facility that both countries can use. Obviously, that’s up to the Colombian government, because it’s a sovereign country that has the right to choose who enters its territory. In terms of a meeting between the presidents, the President would love it. He’s a big fan of the Tiger, as he calls him, and he’d like to meet with him. As you know, the President made a promise-your president here in Colombia-that he wouldn’t travel abroad. So, I would have to bring President Trump to Colombia. Anything is possible. It’s not scheduled at this time, but they’ve already spoken on the phone a couple of times, and I know the President is very enthusiastic about his election and what this could mean for the relationship between both countries. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Will the visas of former Colombian government officials continue to be reviewed in order to cancel those visas of people who are against? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) That’s a normal process. If I have evidence that someone is a criminal, or that someone is engaging in corruption within a country, or that someone is obstructing U.S. foreign policy, harming U.S. interests, or harming the interests of a U.S. ally, we can always suspend a visa. So that happens all over the world, and it will continue to happen here as well. I don’t have any announcement for you today, but I can tell you that if there is evidence here of someone who is doing harm, or has done harm in the past, or who is corrupt, a criminal, or a delinquent, we will take their visa. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Regarding the issue of migration, many of the people who currently reside here in Colombia are part of this population. The president had announced operations starting in Barranquilla, and today he reiterated that the US strategy could be extended to our country. From your perspective, what is your view on this proposal by the president, and what role will the United States play in this matter? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish) I only know what the president has told me, what I’ve seen, that is, publicly. And what he’s said is very clear. I share that view personally and as a public official. We are not against immigration. It needs to be immigration that is controlled, orderly, and legal, through a process, and what no country in the world can allow is for someone to enter without permission. That is extremely dangerous. That is not sustainable. Look at what’s happening in Spain right now. Look at what’s happening in Europe, because for years they let people enter without any permission. And when you enter one European country, you’ve already entered every country in Europe. No country in the world can sustain that. So, every country in the world has immigration laws. The difference is between countries that comply with the law and countries that don’t. I believe that Colombia has faced a lot of pressure due to various events that have occurred in the region. When other countries in the region have been destabilized, people have come in, and these are decent people, not bad people. But no country can take in millions and millions of people, or hundreds of thousands of people, coming in without any controls. So that’s what I’ve heard your President say, which aligns with what President Trump has said as well. QUESTION: Secretary, do you have a (inaudible) of President Trump at the United Nations for the General Assembly later this month? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yes. QUESTION: The UN has warned about potential for a humanitarian crisis in Cuba because of the lack of oil and electricity, and is it a concern in terms of the impact on the Cuban people, the average Cuban person? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, but – yeah, of course, but the problem is – the reason why Venezuela has – I mean Cuba has a lack of oil is because Venezuela doesn’t give them free oil anymore. Understand they were getting free oil from Venezuela. They were stealing oil from Venezuela and they were getting it for free. Some of it they wouldn’t – they would use about 30 percent of it for their own needs and then they would resell the rest of it for cash, and that stopped. So that’s number one. That’s the number one reason why Cuba is having an energy crisis, is because Venezuela no longer gives away their oil for free, which was what was happening. The second reason is they were having blackouts before that. Even with the Venezuelan oil, Cuba had multiple blackouts over the last three or four years because they didn’t invest a penny into their own energy infrastructure. Their economic model doesn’t work. Cuba – if Cuba is a humanitarian catastrophe – and we’ve offered them $100 million of humanitarian aid. Others have as well. No one’s impeding that from coming in. If Cuba is a humanitarian disaster, it is because their government, their regime is a disaster, because the economic model they follow doesn’t work. In fact, it’s nonsensical, because they don’t allow a private sector to flourish, because they don’t allow individual Cubans to choose their own path in life. So I think it’s important to remind everybody this did not start last week. Cuba has been a humanitarian catastrophe now for three or four years, and maybe even longer, because they didn’t invest in their own infrastructure, they stole all the money to build hotels and line their own pockets, and because they’re no longer stealing oil from Venezuela for free. QUESTION: (In Spanish.) Are we going to see in Cuba what we saw in Venezuela? A similar operation to the one that took place there? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) I’m not going to talk about operations. What I can say is that the Cuban case and the Venezuelan case are different, because all cases are different. In the case of Venezuela, it was very specific; there was an individual wanted for… who wasn’t the head of state recognized by us and not recognized by Europe. Nor by many other countries. And he was also a fugitive, a fugitive from U.S. justice who even had ties to drug trafficking. That was the operation in Venezuela. In the case of Cuba, it’s a different case, but a tragic one. A very regrettable, very sad case. But all the blame lies with (inaudible). In Cuba, it has been a humanitarian disaster for more than ten, fifteen years, but specifically in the last year, for one reason: because they can’t keep stealing Venezuela’s oil. In Venezuela, under Maduro, they sold it to line their own pockets. They only used a percentage of that oil. But they had blackouts before, even when they were receiving aid from Venezuela, when they were stealing Venezuelan oil. They were already having blackouts. Because they haven’t invested a single cent in that country’s electrical grid, they haven’t invested a single cent. What they do invest is in ways to oppress the people QUESTION: (In Spanish.) What is going to happen with the elections in Venezuela? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) Are we still live? QUESTION: (In Spanish.) We are live. Yes, sir. What’s going to happen with the elections in-? SECRETARY RUBIO: (In Spanish.) You are a very aggrieve journalist. Go ahead. QUESTION: What is going to happen with the elections in Venezuela? And the second question is, when will the United States ambassador arrive in our country, in Colombia? SECRETARY RUBIO: (in Spanish) Well, we would like to have an ambassador here as soon as possible. That has to go through a process in our Senate. Regarding the elections in Venezuela, that has to happen. Obviously, at this moment we have negotiations-that is, negotiations-but it’s really a process of reconciliation and transition between the 2015 National Assembly, which was the last assembly we recognized as democratically elected, and the country’s interim authorities. And they have progressed quite well. They have to continue progressing. Obviously, to have elections, you have to have institutions: you have to have a Supreme Court, you have to have a National Electoral Committee, you have to have voting machines, you have to have political parties, you have to have a free and open press so that candidates can run and express themselves. All the necessary institutions. So, that has to be built at the same time as we are rebuilding what is…helping Venezuela to have an economic reconstruction. It also has to have a civic reconstruction, a reconstruction of institutions that allow for valid elections, and that as soon as possible, from my point of view. But it has to be done properly. Otherwise, you’ll have another mess. And nobody wants that when it comes to Venezuelans. Thank you very much. QUESTION: (Inaudible) you brought it to he president earlier, advocated for it (inaudible)? SECRETARY RUBIO: No, I think there was an opportunity, that it was an opportunity to bring stability. QUESTION: But you were – you first brought it to f and, like, told him that I think it’s a good idea but (inaudible)? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I told them there was a possibility, among other possibilities, to help the Venezuelan oil industry recuperate. Understand that the Venezuelan oil industry was nonfunctional. It was largely controlled by PDVSA, most of its fields were unproductive, the little they produced was being stolen and sold below market rate. None of it was benefiting the Venezuelan people, and a lot of the fields that were sitting there inactive and unused, their lease rights were being held by Chinese, Russian, and even Iranian companies. So as part of reconstructing Venezuela, you have to professionalize that industry. In this particular case, you had the largest private operator that offered the United States an equity position in the company and access to 20 percent of the production at cost, and it was an opportunity to help these fields come online much faster and produce royalties and revenues that will ultimately go into the hands of Venezuelan authorities but a democratically elected Venezuela in the future. I don’t think there’s any mystery that a core component of reconstruction and rebuilding Venezuela will involve revenues from their energy, but you have to have that through a normal, systemized way, not through the system they had before in which the fields were unproductive and the profits, to the extent there were profits, were being stolen by individuals linked to the government instead of being provided – paying royalties to the government and benefiting the people of the country. QUESTION: Did you meet with or speak with Alejandro Betancourt? SECRETARY RUBIO: I’ve spoken to him before, but ultimately, that deal was negotiated through the Department of War because they have the ability to hold equity positions in companies. It’s a phenomenal deal. It’s an extraordinary deal that’s going to benefit the United States, no doubt about it. I work for the United States of America. That’s who I work for. My job is to further the national interest of the United States, and this deal furthers the national interest of the United States in terms of energy security. But it’s also beneficial to the people of Venezuela because those fields are going to produce more than they could have without our involvement. They’re going to generate royalties and revenues that are going to go into government coffers, not into the pockets of individuals, and ultimately you will have a democratically elected government in Venezuela that will benefit from those royalties to rebuild that country so that its people can once again benefit from the richness of the country, not corrupt individuals or narco-trafficking rings. All right, thanks. Tags Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs Colombia Office of the Spokesperson Official Domestic Travel The Secretary of State

title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio with José Manuel of RCN
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio with José Manuel of RCN Interview Marco Rubio, Secretary of State September 8, 2026 Via Teleconference September 9, 2026 (Via translation.) QUESTION: Well, it is a tremendous honor to have with us here at RCN and NTN24 the United States Secretary of State, Marco Rubio. Secretary, thank you for being here with us. SECRETARY RUBIO: No, thanks. It’s a great honor to be with you as well. QUESTION: They are also watching us in Miami and throughout Latin America thanks to NTN24. As you know, we are networks that have followed your work closely since you were a senator and now as Secretary of State. And now you come to a country like Colombia, one that is not unfamiliar to you, because it must be said that you have defended democracy in our country, Colombia. Additionally, if you’ll allow me a personal question, your wife also has very deep roots in this country. What is your personal connection to Colombia? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, my wife—her mother was born in [inaudible), stayed in [inaudible], and then moved to Bogotá. She still has relatives here. And I live in Miami, and I don’t know if you know this, but there are a lot of Colombians in Miami. QUESTION: Lots of them. SECRETARY RUBIO: And that’s why I wanted to mention it. And in Broward as well. But I have always followed Colombia very closely for two reasons. The personal connection is always important, and we follow everything that happens in the country very closely because of that relationship, but also because of the relationship between our two countries. You have to understand that for more than 20 years, throughout my entire time in the Senate, for example, the most important partner we had in South America was Colombia, the most consistent one. There were changes of government in different places, but when it came to economic and security matters, the most important partner the United States had was Colombia. That was broken over the last four years. Unfortunately, although many relationships still existed at the military and security levels and so forth, we went through a period that, I would say, was not natural in our relationship. It was somewhat damaged, unfortunately. But now we are entering a new stage, and I believe we are quickly going to recover what we had—and not simply recover what we had. We are going to be able to expand it even further, because you have a president here who has tremendous enthusiasm, a lot of energy, a lot of vision, and who is willing to take risks, but who is also responsible and knows the American system well. He understands well how our system works. That is also going to help him greatly in building that connection. QUESTION: In fact, I remember you saying, “The best days are yet to come for Colombia,” after your meeting with Abelardo de la Espriella, and I imagine you still feel the same way. But for that to happen, we need cooperation, especially on an issue that I know has long been a concern for both you and the President: security. How do you view the security situation in Colombia? SECRETARY RUBIO: I have said it, and I will continue to say it. The most important responsibility of any government, at any level—municipal, departmental, state, as we say in the United States, or at the federal or national level—is security. It is the most important thing the government does: security. The security of a country, the security of a community, the security, the security of its people, and that is the most important thing. And to a certain extent, I think that was somewhat neglected in the thinking of the previous government over the last three or four years. You have a president who was very clearly elected, who made it very clear during his campaign and has made it clear now as president that his number one priority is to restore stability and security for the Colombian people, and we are going to help in every way possible. On top of that foundation of security comes prosperity. Prosperity is impossible without security. It is impossible to invest in a country that is unsafe. It is impossible to invest in a country that is dominated by cartels or criminal gangs. In many cases, these are not just Colombian criminal gangs; they are transnational, operating in Ecuador, Mexico, and other countries in the region. So, for us, security is fundamental. It is the most fundamental thing a government does, and these threats affect us as well, so we are going to help in every way possible. But it is not just about security; it is about security and prosperity. The two go together. QUESTION: Look, Secretary, we are being attacked with drones by illegal armed groups, and in that regard, support with technology and upgrading equipment that is already obsolete in Colombia is very important. But there is another issue that is also of great concern, and that is the attacks coming from the other side of the border. You know that Venezuela has granted impunity to many of those criminals. What can the United States do on both fronts? Technological and Venezuela. And the criminals? SECRETARY RUBIO: Let’s talk first about the situation in Venezuela. We have the ELN and the president of the FARC operating openly and with impunity from Venezuelan territory. This has been going on for more than 10, 15 years. That has to be resolved. We have made that clear to the interim authorities in Venezuela, and I think that is going to be key to improving relations between the two countries. It is impossible for relations to truly improve while that issue remains as it is. No country can allow criminal gangs and terrorists to operate with impunity on the other side of its border, attack within its national territory, and then return under the protection of another country’s borders. That cannot be allowed, and we are going to help with that. And we have already spoken with the Venezuelan authorities, including on the issue of drones. The technology is a global threat. This is a global threat because there is a lot of military equipment that requires a government with millions of dollars in order to acquire it. But in the case of these drones, that really is not necessary. Even criminal gangs can possess them and use them to attack and threaten a state. So, one of the things that is needed worldwide, not just in Colombia, is to establish new, modern defenses against this new threat, specifically drones that use fiber optics, which pose an enormous danger because at this time there is no conventional defense against them. So we have already had discussions about that. QUESTION: And is the United States willing to help Colombia? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yes, but we are not only willing to help Colombia; we also need it for our own resources. So, both countries have an interest in developing the new technology necessary to prevent this type of attack and defend against it. QUESTION: Secretary, during the previous administration of President Gustavo Petro, the United States decertified us in the fight against drugs. How close are we to, or how far are we from, being certified again? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, remember that the certification announced this year has to do with the actions that took place last year. We have a completely different view when it comes to the new president and the new administration, this team. So I expect that if they continue to follow through and continue doing what they say they are going to do and what they have already done—I mean, in the last month we have seen more concrete action against these criminal groups than we possibly saw in four years. So I think that if they continue on that path, there is no doubt that the certification will change, as it has in the past. QUESTION: How soon or how far away is that? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, that’s done on an annual basis. It’s possible that it can be done earlier because there’s a waiver process to be able to do it sooner. QUESTION: Are you going to help us in that, I imagine? SECRETARY RUBIO: I, I, what I—I’m going to do everything possible to help Colombia. And obviously, if the new government continues as it already is, it’s not that they’re making promises; they’re already doing it, and they have begun acting against that. I expect that to change. QUESTION: Secretary, there is another issue that is also of great concern to small, large, and medium-sized businesses, and I’m sure it has come up in the conversations you have had over the past month and in the one you had today in Barranquilla. The issue of tariffs on certain products is affecting us. Uh, they are asking for a temporary suspension of some of those tariffs. Are you leaving us with that good news, or are we not there yet? SECRETARY RUBIO: The tariffs, first of all, apply to everyone. They are not specifically directed at Colombia. This is worldwide. The Supreme Court and its ruling against the President’s policy required a change in strategy and the use of a new process, Section 302, which is a U.S. domestic process that is very legal, very, very technical. But the President wants to change that. The way this issue can be resolved is through a bilateral agreement between the two countries, and negotiations on that are underway. I believe there have been two rounds of negotiations, they have progressed very well, and I hope that very soon the issue can be resolved through that agreement between the two countries. And for President Trump, it is a priority. He has said so. He wants to follow through and bring this to a conclusion. He wants to reach a bilateral agreement that eliminates the problem we currently have with the tariffs. QUESTION: Well, that’s good. Hopefully that will be the case. Secretary, I know you are very diplomatic, and you are going to tell me that you cannot say much about the OFAC list and former officials such as President Petro, Armando Benedetti, and others. But tell me, are there any ongoing investigations by the United States into that? SECRETARY RUBIO: It’s not that I’m being diplomatic; I cannot offer opinions or comment on investigations, whether active or not. I cannot comment on that. What I can tell you is that with all these sanctions, in our system there is no sanction that is imposed without evidence, and the evidence is not going to be ignored. If there is evidence that someone has committed a crime, is committing a crime, or has caused harm, that will be pursued. That is not up to me. QUESTION: Are there any active investigations underway? SECRETARY RUBIO: I can’t comment on that because investigations are not under my purview. They are handled by the Department of Justice. So, I cannot comment on whether there are or are not. What I can tell you is that no one ends up on the, on the OFAC list because someone made something up. To be placed on the OFAC list, there have to be facts, there has to be evidence, there have to be concrete things that justify that decision. QUESTION: In the case of these officials. SECRETARY RUBIO: And there may possibly be others who are placed on that list at some point, if there is evidence against them as well. QUESTION: Look, on that note, Gustavo Petro used to say that you had misinformed President Donald Trump. Gustavo Petro is no longer in Colombia; he is no longer the president of Colombia. What does Marco Rubio think of Gustavo Petro? SECRETARY RUBIO: I think he is no longer president, and we are going to deal with the president you have. He is someone I have known for several years, since before he entered politics. I joked earlier that he went crazy and got into politics. But he is someone who was elected by the people of this country and someone we are going to work with. QUESTION: Just so you know, President Abelardo responded, “And you’re next.” SECRETARY RUBIO: Something like that, I think. I didn’t quite understand it; I didn’t see it very clearly, but he—but I had already been in politics for many years. He wasn’t a politician; he had never been a politician. He was interested in politics, but he wasn’t a politician. I knew him as a local businessman in Miami, and then he wanted to contribute to his country, he wanted to help his country. He ran for president when no one thought he was going to win, and he won. And now he is president, and he is the one we are going to deal with. I’m not going to dwell on the past. QUESTION: Look, I know time is short. We’re wrapping up now, Secretary, I promise. But let me ask you about a country that is, close to you, which is Cuba, and also about Nicaragua. What can the United States, and the world, do to finally bring those dictatorships to an end? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, as in every country, first, the primary responsibility for changing a system lies with the people of those countries. That is always the case. Obviously, we do not support what is happening, or what they are doing, in Nicaragua, and we have imposed sanctions against individuals, people who are contributing to the situation that currently exists in Nicaragua. When it comes to Cuba, what we are not going to continue allowing is for a military company called GAESA to keep stealing Cuba’s money, and that is why we have imposed the strongest sanctions in the history of our relationship with Cuba. Tragically, the Cuban people are suffering, but they are not suffering because of us. They are suffering for two reasons. First, because the individuals in charge of that regime are following an economic model that does not work and has never worked. But now it does not work because they have become accustomed, for more than 60 years, to living off assistance from abroad. First, it was the Soviet Union, then it was Hugo Chávez, and when the free oil they were stealing from Venezuela ran out, they were left without oil. That is not our fault. That is their fault for not having a functioning market. And second, because some—many of the leaders in Cuba who are currently part of that regime are incompetent. They do not know how to manage the economy, and they are the ones who have directly contributed to the suffering of the Cuban people. But what we are not going to allow is for them to continue evading sanctions in order to benefit themselves at the expense of the Cuban people. QUESTION: And what do you mean by not allowing it? Carrying out an operation like the one in Venezuela? SECRETARY RUBIO: Not allowing it—well, for example, we are already doing that. We have shut down bank accounts. Many, many foreign companies have left Cuba because of these sanctions, and they have left because those companies were partners, they had entered into business dealings with these elements of the regime, and they were enriching themselves. QUESTION: But could tougher measures be coming, Secretary? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I’m not going to speculate about what those measures might be, but we always have the right to operate and take action to protect the national security of the United States. I’m not going to comment specifically on exactly what can be done, but we have an obligation to protect the national security of the United States if a threat arises in Cuba, Venezuela, or anywhere else in the world. QUESTION: Look, one thing: the possibility of having U.S. military bases in Colombia, yes or no? SECRETARY RUBIO: Anything is possible. Obviously, this has to come through—first, we have to be invited, because this is a sovereign country, and the decision has to be made by the Venezuelan people through—sorry, by the Colombian people, through their elected officials. If they officially make that request to us, then it will be considered to see what is possible. At the end of the day, that decision is up to the President, through the U.S. Department of Defense, the Department of War. But what I can tell you, without a doubt, is that the security relationship between the United States and Colombia is not going to be the same as before; it is going to be better. QUESTION: Look, I’ll wrap up, but as we say here in Colombia, President Abelardo de la Espriella gave me the task to ask you about your political future. The 2028 elections. Am I interviewing one of the strongest candidates for 2028? SECRETARY RUBIO: But I’m not a candidate for anything right now, and I’m 100% focused on my job, and I have to be because I have two jobs. I have my job as Secretary of State, and I also work as the President’s National Security Advisor, so I have plenty of work right now. QUESTION: But is the dream of becoming President of the United States there? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time. I’m 100% focused on my jobs. QUESTION: Secretary, and speaking of that job, we want to thank you, on behalf of all Colombians, for what you have done for this country and for its democracy. And please, continue to keep in mind cooperation based on equality, trust, and respect between the United States and Colombia. Thank you, Marco Rubio. SECRETARY RUBIO: Thank you very much. title: Secretary Rubio and Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella at a Strategic Civil Nuclear Cooperation and Critical Minerals Framework Memorandums of Understanding Signing Ceremony
text: hide Secretary Rubio and Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella at a Strategic Civil Nuclear Cooperation and Critical Minerals Framework Memorandums of Understanding Signing Ceremony Remarks Marco Rubio, Secretary of State Batallon Paraiso Barranquilla, Colombia September 8, 2026 MODERATOR: (Via interpreter) Good afternoon. Good afternoon. The Presidency of Colombia and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs would like to welcome you to the – to the ceremony of two memorandums of understanding between the Government of Colombia and the Government of the U.S. of America. We are pleased to have His Highness President Abelardo De La Espriella, who is the president of Colombia, that’s going to be in this act as the witness – as a witness of honor. And we would also like to greet Omar Bula Escobar, who is the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Colombia, and His Excellency Marco Rubio, who is the Secretary of State of the United States of America, who are going to sign both agreements. (In English) Good afternoon. The Presidency of the Republic of Colombia and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs welcome you to the signing ceremony of two memoranda of understanding between the Government of the Republic of Colombia and the Government of the United States of America. We are honored by the presence of His Excellency Abelardo De La Espriella, President of the Republic of Colombia, who joins us as witness of honor. We also welcome His Excellency Omar Bula Escobar, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Colombia, and the Honorable Marco Rubio, Secretary of State of the United States of America, who will sign both instruments. (In Spanish.) (In English) We will now proceed with the signing of the first memorandum of understanding, the Framework Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of Colombia for Securing of Supply in the Mining and Processing of Critical Minerals and Rare Earths. (Applause.) (The Memorandum is signed.) (Applause.) (Via interpreter) Okay, thank you so much. We will now proceed with the signing of the second memorandum of understanding that it’s called the Memorandum of Understanding Between the Government of Colombia and the United States of America about Civil Strategic Cooperation, signed by the chancellor of Colombia and the Secretary of State of the U.S. (In English) We will now proceed with the signing of the second memorandum of understanding, the Memorandum of Understanding Between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of Colombia Concerning Strategic Civil Nuclear Cooperation. (Applause.) (The Memorandum is signed.) (Applause.) (Via interpreter) Thank you so much. Thank you so much. And now we were going to go to the joint declaration about the meeting between the – the statement between Abelardo De La Espriella and the Secretary of State of the United States Marco Rubio. And we’re going to initiate with the Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Mr. Secretary, welcome. Welcome. SECRETARY RUBIO: (Via interpreter) Thank you so much, Mr. President. And thank you. I’m so glad – I’m so glad. I came here last time as a senator but in the last four years as a senator, and then as the Secretary of State we hadn’t traveled here. And I think that until a certain point, this is a signal of the distance that had been created between our governments, which is not natural because the relationship between Colombia and the United States is almost impossible to replicate because they are personal links, cultural links, and also – and also at the economic level. And also we also have the opportunity to restore that natural relationships that we have between our countries, but also to grow into a new stage, a new cooperation stage with our president even stronger than we had before. We talked a lot about security, because always security is key, because without security there is no prosperity. But the opportunities that exist between Colombia and the U.S. is much more than security because it’s the base of everything. Without security it’s impossible to operate as a country and as a society. But beyond that – because sometime people say that I – now they’re telling me I’m speaking in a low – you can hear me well, right? They say I’m speaking in a very low voice. There is no doubt that without security a country cannot progress, and the threats to security that Colombia is facing, it’s the same things that we face in the U.S.: the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people. But that’s the base. That’s the key. That’s the most relevant thing. And because the most important role of any – of any government in any part of the world, it’s the security of its people. But above that, we can build on prosperity, which is extremely important to move forward. And also the opportunity that exists for Colombia at the economic level are huge, are amazing, and these are opportunities that Mr. President has in mind that we can work together so that it benefits both countries. We have a lot to do because, unfortunately, this government inherited a series of disasters, bad decisions, and we feel – we feel the same when we went into power a year and a half ago. But you are facing the errors of the last four years, and you need to face this. And besides that, there was a disaster. There was an earthquake that was tragical. But there are amazing opportunities, and we’re going to use this opportunity that we have nowadays, because the links between our two governments are so solid to ensure that not only are we going to focus on security, but this is something going to be key in our relationship, but we’re also going to focus in what we call the opportunity of creating a prosperity that helps the North American people and also helps the Colombian people. And this relationship between our governments have a – have direct impact on the daily life of people here but also the people in the U.S., and especially people in the certain part of Florida where I’ve lived most of my life. If you allow, Mr. President, I’m going to give a couple of words. (In English) I want to say a few words in English as well. First, I want to thank the president for receiving us. It – it’s not every day – let me say in this in Spanish first. I should’ve said it earlier. (Via interpreter) It’s not – and we’ve not always traveled to a country and we have the opportunity to exchange with chief of state that you met before they were president, before he was a politician, because of the mutual relationships that we have. And even when we were talking not long ago, the two years ago when we were in the same – we were in the same table at a wedding in the southern part of Florida. That’s why this is a place where the president of the – the president is someone that I’ve met at a personal level. And then he went crazy and decided to become a politician and decided to turn president. (In English) So I think that it’s unusual that you travel to a country that you meet with a head of state and a president who you’ve actually known for years before he was president, before he was even in politics. And as I was joking, when he lost his mind and went into politics, and – but he’s going to do a great job for this country, and I know that. I know that from what I know about him from before he was president. This is a man of energy. This is a man of strength. This is a man of vision and of courage because he’s confronting a very difficult situation. He has inherited many disasters. Obviously, the country faces the aftermath of a natural disaster in an earthquake, but he also faces a disaster that’s institutional, that goes through four years of very bad management and that, frankly, harmed the relationship between the United States and Colombia, something that simply is not natural. The United States and Colombia have a strong bond that exists well beyond just the cooperation of our governments. It’s a strong economic bond. It’s a strong cultural bond. It’s a strong people-to-people bond, a social bond. I can tell you personally, having lived in south Florida the majority of my life, how we follow so closely the events that happen in Colombia, because it has a direct impact on life in south Florida and ultimately in our country. This is the natural state of things, is for the U.S. and Colombia to be strong allies and strong partners, and the last four years is an aberration between our governments. But that is changing as well. Clearly, the most important obligation of any government is to provide for the security of their people. It’s the number one obligation, and that is certainly an issue that you will confront here and that I am confident the president and his team are very serious about, and we’re going to do everything we can to help you. But security is the basic and most important requirement of a government, but prosperity follows closely behind it, and that is opportunity of a country and an economy that provides the opportunity for upward mobility and prosperity for all of its people. And we believe we have a lot we can do together in the field of energy, in the field of trade, in the field of commerce, that allows both countries to benefit: the people of the United States, who I work for, and the people of Colombia, who the president works for and his team works for. So I’m excited that after not having been here for a while, to be back, to be back with someone I know so well as president, who I know has a great vision and energy for the future, and excited to be back in a country that has been our strongest ally and partner in the region for many, many years. And we look forward not just to restoring that but building upon it and creating a golden age of relationships between our two countries and our two people. Muchas gracias . (Applause.) PRESIDENT DE LA ESPRIELLA: Thank you. (Via interpreter) A very special welcome to all of you today. Barranquilla has been the scenario of a – of a very strategic conversation for the present and for the future of Colombia and of our relationship with the United States of America. To welcome the Secretary of State Marco Rubio here in the Colombian Caribbean has a very special meaning, because Barranquilla has been historically the Golden Door of Colombia to the world and represents an absolute conviction of my government because Colombia, it’s not just governed from Bogotá, Colombia; it’s governed from its regions. I would like to thank Secretary Rubio. His presence – we are honored by his presence. He has been an inspiration for this battle for democracy, institutionality, and freedom because there is no Latino in the world that doesn’t feel represented by Marco Rubio, that has always done things the best way possible. And with regards to our community, that’s why I thank you so much, Mr. Secretary of State. It’s a pride and honor to have you here in the land of Barranquilla. I also would like to publicly acknowledge the solidarity of the U.S. Government after the earthquake that we endured on August 10th. They have helped us with 26.5 million U.S. dollars in humanitarian assistance, and besides all of what they are doing regarding the fires that people are suffering near Tolima. No country in the world has helped as much as the United States, and today we’re giving a step forward. We are not going back from the solidarity in the emergency, to a very strategic partnership, a long-term strategic partnership. From this meeting there is a guideline that we’ve called the Barranquilla agreements, and they follow three main topics that are highly relevant for our country and for the hemisphere. We are going to rebuild the homeland, we are going to recover the economy, and we are going to protect the hemisphere. And we’re initiating a historical and close relationship that was interrupted during four years, but it has always been there in the deeper areas, in the deeper basis of Colombia, because the United States has been our partner. We have been their ally and partner, and when the United States and Colombia have worked together, the only thing that we have had, it’s development, security, and progress. The main purpose of this agreement, it’s the rebuilding and the economic recovery. The earthquake left huge challenges in households, in bridges, utilities, and in productive capacity. We were thinking where we wanted to work on cooperation, investment, and funding mechanisms, including the – including the International Development Corporation, other agencies, the private sectors and companies from both countries. We would like to attract investments to the infrastructure, energy, households energy, and the productive reconstruction Colombia is also going to do (inaudible) because we are going to do what we have to do regarding fiscal discipline, the legal certainty, efficiency, expanding better investment conditions. In the same way, I requested Mr. Secretary of State to accompany us before multilateral organisms to enable instruments that allow us to fund these transitions without sacrificing the economic transition of our countries. We are proposing to the U.S. a partnership where Colombia puts project territories, productive capabilities, resources, and clear rules and regulations (inaudible) the U.S. supports investments funding technologies and business capability. Other of the important points, it’s shared prosperity. I have proposed Mr. Secretary to have this bilateral prosperity dialogue with very specific projects with – that has funding, timelines that our teams in Washington are going to continue developing. We identified some policies regarding infrastructure, technology, industry, rebuilding, and also rare – and also rare minerals, which is the treatment we’ve just signed. Colombia has access to two oceans, has the strategic resources and human talent. We need to turn all those opportunities that Colombia has in investments and productive chains, in manufacturing and also in employment for our people. Another very important point, it’s security in the struggle against drug terrorism. Colombia wants to become the first hemispheric security partner with the U.S., and we’re going to be the partner number one in South America. The 21st centuries require new capabilities. That’s why we have proposed to the government, and I said it once again today, the Patriot Plan 21st century is to update airplanes, drones, radars, helicopters, anti-drone systems, aerial defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and the maintenance and the operationality. We’re going to have our own resource and we hope to build together capabilities to be able to face sophisticated threats. But at the same time, we need the support – we need the support, a push from the United States, and we’re going to work in a very decisive manner in our fight against drug trafficking. We’re going to start with – we’re going to go through the precursors, we’re going to go through the pathways, we’re going to go through the leaders, we’re going to go to the narc terrorists, we’re going to go through the money laundering and other criminal equity and also those international networks that are a huge challenge not only for the hemisphere but also for humankind. Colombia, it’s ready to have annual quotas, verifiable indicators, and very specific agreements. We’re going to do what we are (inaudible), and with that basis we want to have a co-responsibility that is effective for both countries. Another important thing – it’s the Shield of Americas. We’re already operational. Colombia is going to fulfill its responsibilities. We’re going to have the site in Medellín, and we’re going to do whatever it takes to be able to attack and to be able to give them the place that they deserve, which is either a prison or a tomb. And I say it: If a criminal doesn’t – if a criminal doesn’t follow the law, he is going to – he’s not going to get it his way. And we also talked about Venezuela because we share more than 2,000 kilometers of borders with the neighboring countries, and everything that happens in Venezuela has a direct consequence in Colombia regarding security, migration, smuggling, armed – and armed groups, and also energy. Colombia will participate along with the United States in a very responsible manner in the focused efforts to be able to ensure regional stability and will – and will delve on trans-border cooperation, migration, and security. Our interest, Mr. Secretary of State, it’s that we each have institutionality, stability, and also security. We want to avoid any type of issue. Another very important point that I mentioned to Mr. Secretary, it’s our foreign policy is based on a main policy. It’s that Colombia relates with the world from its own national interests. It has sovereignty, autonomy, pragmatism, and also a long-term vision, and this is where we’re perfectly tuned with the United States. We have now resources, geographic positions, human talent, and also very strategic assets. Our diplomacy needs to turn those strengths in opportunities to be able to become the best partners of the U.S. And we’re going to do it, Mr. Secretary, because this is a new rebirth. Another very important topic, it’s migration and the rule of law. We agreed to delve on migration – more migration cooperation, exchange of information, biometric tools, identifying of the people (inaudible) to struggle against the migrants’ networks, and also the strengthening of border controls. Our idea, it’s that legal migration and – legal, safe, and organized migration, because our principle, it’s the same one that the United States shared. We’re not against migration. We’re against illegal migration, which is something different. And there is a topic that it’s very close to my heart, and I said, Mr. Secretary, you know that many years ago we had – we had a consulate. And I said, hey, as the son of this region, I said if you can please open a consular office in Barranquilla, the alternate capital city of Colombia. And we are – we want a venue. We would like to consider it if possible, Mr. Secretary, because it’s been something that we’ve expected for years. First we had a consular office in Barranquilla, and then they took – and they removed the one from Barranquilla. The idea, it’s to go back to things as were before, and we hope to have here in (inaudible) Barranquilla the American consular office. And once again, a topic that it’s also close to my heart, it’s cooperation to follow the path of the money. We would like to – we would like to see what’s money laundering resources that come from resources and hidden assets, strengthening judicial cooperation and financial cooperation. All of this, it’s going to be under the evidence of the framework of law, due process, and the respect for institutions, because to catch criminals, it’s not enough. We also need to strike the money that supports those financial structures. We need to affect the pocket of the criminals because it will hurt them. This was a very deep, cordial, strategic conversation. Not only are we talking about the United States can do for Colombia, we also talked about what Colombia and the United States can do together for the hemisphere, because Colombia contributes a geographic position, strategic resources, productive capability, human talent, a very experienced armed forces, and a government that is committed. And we would – wanted this – this new stage to start here in Barranquilla, in the Colombian Caribbean, and in the region. The Barranquilla agreements need to turn into projects, investments, and cooperation. In the security and also specific outcomes, we need to rebuild the homeland. We need to recover the economy. We need to protect the hemisphere. As of now, our teams (inaudible) will start to work to turn those expectations, those desires, those projects, and realities. May God bless the United States of America. May God bless Colombia hoy more than ever. (Inaudible.) Thank you. (Applause.) MODERATOR: (Via interpreter) Thank you so much, Mr. President. Thank you so much, Mr. Secretary of State. We – in this way, we are fulfilling the agenda of Mr. Marco Rubio to the (inaudible) and city of Barranquilla. Thank you so much. title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to Press
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to Press Remarks Marco Rubio, Secretary of State Homestead Air Reserve Base Homestead, Florida September 8, 2026 SECRETARY RUBIO: So this is an important trip, obviously. We’re going to go visit three countries strongly aligned with the United States. We have a lot of common interests with them, both taking on regional transnational criminal terrorism and also economic engagements. We’re hoping to wrap up good, solid trade deals with all three of these countries in the foreseeable future. And of course, a lot of strong cultural links. So I think it’s part of a trend that you’re seeing in the Western Hemisphere of alignment with the U.S. and U.S. interests. If you read our National Security Strategy – I’m sure all of you have read it very carefully page by page – it outlines one of our priorities is strengthening our presence in the Western Hemisphere. And I think this trip and these meetings, as much as anything else, is continuing to further that goal as part of that strategy. QUESTION: Secretary Rubio, why not travel to Venezuela on this trip? As you mentioned, this is all about the Western Hemisphere. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we’ll get there eventually, as I said, but you can’t go everywhere. This is a condensed week, obviously, with Labor Day yesterday and then 9/11 on – on Friday that we’ll be commemorating the 25th anniversary. So we just simply couldn’t add another, and these are countries we needed to get to that I hadn’t gotten to yet. So in the case of Colombia, they just had a free and democratic election. They elected someone I know very well, very aligned with the U.S., and we want to – we have a longstanding relationship. In the case of Peru, after some political turmoil, they too have had a recent election, and President Fujimori is someone we look forward to engaging with. And then in Ecuador, obviously, their election was last year but they face – they’re one of our closest security partners in the region, and I think there’s more we can do with them – economics as well. QUESTION: Secretary Rubio, what would your message be to Latin Americans who might look at the Venezuela oil deal and think that the U.S. Government’s interested in extracting resources or just sending troops? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I — QUESTION: What’s your message? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, what I would say to anyone who is concerned that the U.S. is doing something negative towards the Western Hemisphere as regards to energy is those oil fields, once dominated by China and Russia and Iran, by the way; Iran also had some concessions – and they’re no longer there. So I think they’re much better off partnering with the United States. They will benefit greatly from it. These fields were in many cases nonproductive; in essence, the Chinese and Russian companies held these fields but never turned them into anything. These fields are going to be productive and they’re going to generate royalties and revenues for the Venezuelan people – eventually through a democratically elected government, hopefully sooner rather than later – and directly benefit the people of Venezuela, as opposed to going into the pocket of some corrupt government official or in the hands of American and Venezuelan adversaries, really. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, do you have anything to say about the British decision on the imports from Israel – or from settlements in — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, they alerted us to it. We don’t have any announcements. Obviously, these are decisions that they make. And we and the President has expressed this in the past: We don’t want to see anything destabilizing going on right now in the West Bank with so much going on in the region. We think it has implications as well on our ability to make progress with regards to Gaza and the 20-point plan and Board of Peace that we’re very committed to. Obviously, we’re not going to do what the UK did. We saw their announcement today, but I don’t have any comment on it right now. QUESTION: But Ambassador Huckabee said that you’ve – that the Brits will suffer because of that with the U.S., that he suggested that the U.S. — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I would say that the President has not commented on this. As I said, neither have I at this point. We were made aware that they were going to make this decision. We heard their arguments as to why. But look, we share the goal of stability. We don’t want to see some uptick in violence or an uptick in conflict or tensions in the West Bank at a very tenuous time in the region. There’s always tenuous times. But beyond that, I don’t think – as of this moment, we don’t have any further comment on the UK decision that I think was announced just a few hours ago. QUESTION: Overnight the Houthis launched a substantial attack on Saudi Arabia. What are your thoughts on that when the U.S. has put pressure on the Houthis to kind of stay out of this fight? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, look, again, the Houthis in many ways are agents and proxies of the Iranians. I think behind some of this is clearly the Iranian hand. The U.S. has a very strong defensive military relationship with Saudi Arabia, and we’re watching those events very closely. It’s been going on for some time. I think there’s been some ground operations as well where many forces are taking on the Houthis and pushing back against some of the ground advances that they attempted to make. And we’re monitoring that, as I said, very, very closely. And – but I would defer as far as on the defense side to the Department of War. I don’t think there’ll be any announcements on that today. title: 200 Days of Action
text: hide 200 Days of Action Other Release Office of the Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism July 22, 2026 Ambassador Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun was sworn in as the U.S. Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism on December 22, 2025. Just over 200 days into office, Ambassador Kaploun has been working to make Americans and Jewish communities globally safer, stronger, and more prosperous. Ambassador Kaploun addresses attendees at America’s 250th Birthday Shabbat Dinner. Combated antisemitic terrorists Spearheaded an interagency effort to arrest Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, a radical Islamist who claimed responsibility for multiple attacks and attempted plots throughout Europe and the United States. Convened interagency officials and NGOs for the first-ever Symposium on Islamist Ideology and Antisemitism. Safeguarded Jewish sites and institutions Secured commitments from Belgium , the Netherlands, and more than half a dozen other governments across Europe and Latin America to increase security measures following the wave of terrorist attacks on Jewish sites and institutions in the spring of 2026. Held governments accountable Introduced a consequences-based approach at the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and the Special Envoys and Coordinators Combatting Antisemitism (SECCA) Forum. Engaged closely with Australian officials to promote transparency and action in the aftermath of the Bondi Beach attack – the deadliest antisemitic terrorist attack since October 7, 2023. Advanced accurate Holocaust remembrance and education Secured Armenia’s willingness to join the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) alongside several Latin American governments. Represented the U.S. at the Jasenovac concentration camp and Donja Gradina memorial sites. Addressed thousands of Jewish youth, survivors, and international law enforcement at the March of the Living at Auschwitz-Birkenau. Enhanced monitoring capabilities Introduced new reporting requirements for U.S. embassies to monitor antisemitic incidents abroad, establishing a framework to collect information and hold perpetrators of antisemitic violence, including associated acts of terrorism, accountable. Strengthened diplomatic engagement Held high-level meetings with foreign ministers and other senior officials from across Europe, Latin America, Asia, and the Middle East to enhance international cooperation and elevate the fight against global antisemitism as a national security priority. Celebrated 250 years of Jewish American heritage and culture Convened foreign ambassadors, senior U.S. officials, and Jewish community leaders for America’s 250 th Birthday Shabbat Dinner. Engaged interfaith communities Expanded diplomatic partnerships through high-level meetings with foreign ministers and ambassadors from across the Middle East. Addressed interfaith gatherings, including the Muslim World League, Christians United for Israel (CUFI), and the Israel Allies Foundation. Hosted a traditional Shabbat dinner for more than 80 ambassadors, U.S. officials and Jewish community leaders to promote dialogue for Jews, Christians, Muslims, and people of all faiths. Ambassador Kaploun meets with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud at the Munich Security Conference. Photo credit: Saudi Press Agency. Ambassador Kaploun meets with UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan. Photo credit: Office of the UAE Minister of Foreign Affairs. Ambassador Kaploun addresses a commemoration at the Donja Gradina site in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Photo credit: U.S. Embassy Sarajevo. Ambassador Kaploun congratulates President Javier Milei on Argentina’s successful IHRA presidency. Photo credit: Oficina del Presidente de La República Argentina. Ambassador Kaploun co-hosts with Ambassador of Argentina Alec Oxenford a commemoration marking the 32nd anniversary of the terrorist attack on the AMIA Jewish community center in Buenos Aires. Photo credit: Embassy of the Argentine Republic to the USA.
