title: Quad Sherpas’ Meeting in New Delhi
text: hide Quad Sherpas’ Meeting in New Delhi Media Note Office of the Spokesperson September 3, 2026 India’s Foreign Secretary Shri Vikram Misri hosted a Quad Sherpas’ Meeting in New Delhi on 3 rd September 2026. The meeting was attended by Ms. Elly Lawson, Deputy Secretary, Strategic Planning & Coordination Group, Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, Australia; Mr. Hiroyuki Namazu, Senior Deputy Minister for Foreign Affairs, Japan; and Mr. Sergio Gor, Special Envoy to South and Central Asia and Ambassador of USA to India. The Quad Sherpas’ Meeting follows the Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting held in New Delhi on 26 th May 2026 and was convened to take forward its outcomes and to prepare for the next Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting. The Sherpas reviewed progress across ongoing Quad initiatives and discussed ways to further strengthen practical cooperation, with a shared commitment to advancing a free and open Indo-Pacific . Discussions covered key areas of Quad cooperation, including maritime and transnational security; economic prosperity and security; critical and emerging technologies; and humanitarian assistance and emergency response. The Sherpas also exchanged views on developments in the Indo-Pacific and the broader regional and global context. The Quad Sherpas reaffirmed the importance of focusing on concrete, action-oriented initiatives. They looked forward to continued consultations in the lead-up to the next Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting. title: Further Sanctions on Cuba’s Elites, Financial Channels, and Resource Exploitation Apparatus
text: hide Further Sanctions on Cuba’s Elites, Financial Channels, and Resource Exploitation Apparatus Press Statement Marco Rubio, Secretary of State September 3, 2026 The Communist Cuban regime continues to pose a deep, multifaceted threat to U.S. national security and our hemisphere’s stability. While the Cuban people suffer, the Castro family and their cronies in Cuba’s repressive Ministry of the Interior (MININT) continue to perpetuate their total control of the island’s economy, hoarding resources for the benefit of a small group of regime elites. Today, pursuant to President Trump’s Executive Order (E.O.) 14404, “Imposing Sanctions on Those Responsible for Repression in Cuba and for Threats to United States National Security and Foreign Policy,” I am designating five entities and one individual whose activities prop up the regime’s financial services, metals and mining, and energy sectors, and are part of networks that advance the regime’s threats to U.S. national security. Among those designated today are a grandson of Raúl Castro, Fidel Ernesto Castro Calis, Banco Exterior de Cuba, and four entities exploiting Cuba’s natural resources or energy reserves for the benefit of the regime. These designations reflect President Trump’s unwavering vision for a free Cuba — one where the regime’s illicit financial networks, repressive apparatuses, and entrenched Castro-era power structures are dismantled, and where the Cuban people, not their oppressors, inherit the nation’s future. The Department’s actions are being taken pursuant to E.O. 14404, which authorizes sweeping sanctions on Cuba, including against persons who support the Cuban regime’s security apparatus and those responsible for repression in Cuba and other threats to U.S. national security. These actions also further both E.O. 14380, “ Addressing Threats to the United States by the Government of Cuba ” and National Security Presidential Memorandum 5 , which directs the Executive Branch to improve human rights, encourage the rule of law, foster free markets and free enterprise, and promote democracy in Cuba. For more information on today’s action, see the Department of State’s Fact Sheet . title: Further Sanctions on Cuba’s Elites, Financial Channels, and Resource Exploitation Apparatus
text: hide Further Sanctions on Cuba’s Elites, Financial Channels, and Resource Exploitation Apparatus Fact Sheet Office of the Spokesperson September 3, 2026 Today, the Department of State is designating five entities and one individual to further the Trump Administration’s comprehensive push to end the Cuban regime’s malign activities, both in Cuba and across our hemisphere. This action includes imposing sanctions on an additional member of the Castro family and further restricts the regime’s ability to fund and resource its repression. All Department of State targets sanctioned today have been designated pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 14404, which authorizes sanctions on foreign persons determined to meet specified criteria related to repression in Cuba and other threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy. Continued Designations of the Castro Regime FIDEL ERNESTO CASTRO CALIS (CASTRO CALIS) , grandson of Raul Modesto Castro Ruz, is being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(I) of E.O. 14404 for being an adult family member of ALEJANDRO CASTRO ESPIN (CASTRO ESPIN), a person designated pursuant to this order. CASTRO ESPIN, who is CASTRO CALIS’s father, was designated alongside CASTRO CALIS’s brother, RAUL ALEJANDRO CASTRO CALIS, pursuant to E.O. 14404 on June 4, 2026. Further Restricting the Regime’s Ability to Exploit the International Financial System BANCO EXTERIOR DE CUBA , a Cuban state-owned bank that specializes in corporate banking, foreign-trade finance, and international transactions, is being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(A) of E.O. 14404 for operating in or having operated in the financial services sector of the Cuban economy. Cuban Entities Exploiting the Metals and Mining Sector The following entities associated with the exploitation of Cuba’s metals and mining sector for the regime’s benefit are being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(A) of E.O. 14404 for operating in or having operated in the metals and mining sector of the Cuban economy: EMPRESA DE SERVICIOS COMANDANTE RENE RAMOS LATOUR (NICAROTEC) , which is a Cuban state-owned industrial and technical services enterprise which provides geological and mining support for the Cuban nickel sector. EMPRESA IMPORTADORA Y ABASTECEDORA DEL NIQUEL (CEXNI) , a foreign-trade and logistics enterprise that imports and supplies specialized raw materials, machinery, and equipment for Cuba’s nickel and cobalt industry. Cuban Entities Exploiting the Energy Sector The following entities associated with the exploitation of Cuba’s energy sector for the regime’s benefit are designated: EMPRESA IMPORTADORA DE ABASTECIMIENTO PARA EL PETROLEO (ABAPET) is being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(B) of E.O. 14404 for being owned, controlled, or directed by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, UNION CUBA PETROLEO (CUPET), a person whose property or interests in property are blocked pursuant to this order. ABAPET is a CUPET subsidiary that primarily engages in procurement support activities for CUPET, and has specifically imported technological equipment, spare parts, specialized tools, and industrial inputs required to sustain Cuba’s energy sector. COMERCIAL CUPET S.A. is being designated pursuant to Sec. 2(a)(i)(A) of E.O. 14404 for operating in or having operated in the energy sector of the Cuban economy. COMERCIAL CUPET S.A. is a Cuban state-owned entity which represents CUPET in negotiations and joint ventures with foreign entities. Sanctions Implications As a result of today’s sanctions actions, and in accordance with E.O. 14404 of May 1, 2026, “Imposing Sanctions on Those Responsible for Repression in Cuba and for Threats to U.S. National Security and Foreign Policy,” all property and interests in property of the designated persons described above that are in the United States or in possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). Additionally, all entities that are owned individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked. All transactions and dealings by U.S. persons or persons within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of designated or otherwise blocked persons are prohibited unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC or exempt. These prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any blocked person and the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person. Foreign persons that engage in transactions with persons designated pursuant to E.O. 14404—or that operate or have operated in the energy, defense and related materiel, metals and mining, financial services, or security sector of the Cuban economy, as identified in E.O. 14404— are themselves at risk of sanctions. Non-U.S. persons, including foreign financial institutions, should proceed with caution in any dealings with a party sanctioned under this authority. Actions to return assets to a sanctioned party or transfer them to another jurisdiction for potential use by the target expose non-U.S. persons to significant sanctions risk. All property and interests in property of persons that are blocked pursuant to the Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR) continue to be blocked. The CACR prohibits persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction from dealing in property in which Cuba or a Cuban national has an interest, unless authorized or exempt. The power and integrity of U.S. government sanctions derive not only from the U.S. government’s ability to designate and add persons to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List consistent with the law. The ultimate goal of sanctions is not to punish, but to bring about a positive change in behavior. Petitions for removal from the SDN List may be routed through OFAC’s Reconsiderations Portal . Petitioners may also refer to the Department of State’s Delisting Guidance page . title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the Trump Administration’s Foundry School Launch
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the Trump Administration’s Foundry School Launch Remarks Marco Rubio, Secretary of State Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace Washington, D.C. September 3, 2026 UNDER SECRETARY HELBERG: Every so often, history hands a nation a choice: to drift, or to build. And every so often, it hands that nation a leader who inspires people to reject the drifters and build with boldness and confidence in the future. One of our guests this morning is the son of Cuban exiles, a man whose family fled a regime that confiscated everything, and who grew up understanding in his bones that freedom and prosperity are not inherited – they’re defended, and they’re built. That heritage made him clear-eyed, and it gave him something rare in Washington: the memory of what it costs when a country loses its future. For decades in the United States Senate, he warned us. He warned us that we traded our industrial base for the illusion of cheap abundance. He warned us that supply chains had become weapons pointed at us. And this year in Munich, in a speech that will be studied for a generation, he said what no Secretary of State had dared to say – that deindustrialization was a choice, and that reindustrialization must now be ours. He called on the free world not merely to defend Western civilization but to build a new Western century. Under President Trump’s leadership, he has turned that vision into policy, restoring American economic strength as the foundation of economic power, and reminding the world that the arsenal of democracy was never a metaphor – it was a factory floor. He’s a statesman, a patriot, and the driving force behind the most consequential renewal of American economic statecraft since the Second World War. Ladies and gentlemen, please join me in welcoming the 72nd Secretary of State of the United States, Secretary Marco Rubio. (Applause.) SECRETARY RUBIO: Thank you. Thank you, all of you, first of all, for being here today. Thank you – Jacob Helberg’s doing a phenomenal job. Everybody at our department is doing a great job, and I’m very proud of the work the State Department is putting in into these and other initiatives. One of the things we really wanted to do in our time here, and one of the reasons behind many of the reforms we undertook, is to allow us to have a State Department that could move at the speed of relevance, which is something we used to say all the time. Now it’s become almost a cliche, but it really is important – because world affairs are moving so quickly, economic developments are moving so quickly, and so much of that is internationalized, and it involves what we do around the world as well. And so, I’m very proud of everybody at the Department of State and all the work that they’re doing to be a part of this initiative, along with our partners in the other agencies, because this truly is an interagency challenge that we’re facing. What is the challenge that we’re here to talk about today? Let me put it to you this way: I think we made a terrible mistake in this country – not – many years ago, under people that were in charge at the time, especially at the end of the Cold War. And that was the idea that the ability to make things no longer mattered. And no matter – it didn’t matter any longer where things were made. They were to be made in the most efficient place at the lowest possible cost. That meant more profits for the company, lower costs for the consumers, and that was the way the world would work. There was this fantasy, really, that the whole world would become a free enterprise, democracies, and that everyone would look us. That ran into reality – the reality that that is not how human events have ever worked, that the nation-state still does matter, nationalism is still real, national borders still matter, and that countries are going to always act in their best interest. But the result of it is that it deindustrialized America. We lost our ability and our capacity to make things, and not just big things – not just the kinds of big machinery and things that we normally identify with industry – but even some of the most basic components that are necessary, that underpin economic life, especially in the 21st century. And we woke up to the reality just a few years ago that we are suddenly, as a nation, dangerously dependent – dangerously dependent – on other nations for all sorts of things that we need, not simply for our economic vibrancy but, in many cases, for our national security and our very survival as a prosperous nation-state. And so now we are involved in this endeavor across the board to try to reverse those mistakes. And it will be the work of multiple administrations, but it starts here and it starts now with this one that is receiving attention at its highest level. One way is just the basic ingredients that go into all this, and it’s why you’ve seen such a focus on access to not just critical minerals as raw material but also to the ability to process them. But the other is – has to be the ability to actually make things once again. And we have to understand that re-industrialization, that 21st century industrial activity is going to look different than it did in the 20th century. It’s going to involve far more skills. It’s going to involve – not just are our workers going to have to be better educated in what they’re doing, but in many cases, given the evolution and the rapidly changing dynamics of the modern world, they may have to be retrained multiple times in their career. One of the crown jewels that have powered American innovation and, ultimately, powered American economic influence and power around the world has been our system of higher education. It has produced extraordinary research; it has produced extraordinary breakthroughs. I think the sad part about it is the number of things we have innovated or created, but then they’re made somewhere else. And so, I think in the 21st century, this partnership with higher education is important, and it’s important for two reasons. First of all, why build it when – why build a new wheel when we already have a wheel? We just need to repurpose that wheel to become the place where 21st century American workers go to become empowered with the skills they need to succeed. But I also think it’s important for higher education, and we’ve got some great partners here today that are already part of this initiative, and, of course, we want this partnership to grow to include other schools as well. But I think it’s also important for higher education because, increasingly, young Americans are asking: Is the college degree worth it? Is the college route worth it? Because we have to borrow money or we have to spend money or we have to do all these sorts of things and, in the end, I get a degree, and all that degree does is either a) qualify me to get another degree or b) it may not even really lead to a job necessarily that’s different from the one I could have gotten otherwise. And I think this speaks to that, because it also – in addition to being good for our country – is an opportunity to say to students: If you come here and you go to school and you follow this curriculum, you will leave here not just with a paper credential but with the skills that make you immediately employable in a high-paying job, in a good-paying job with long-term stability. And so this partnership is critical because what I hope it means, what I hope it symbolizes – and not just symbolizes but what I hope it is evidence of – is how government partnering with non-government entities like our higher education system and the private sector, the combination of those three pillars – the private sector that needs the workers and knows what they need from the workers; the higher education system that can equip young Americans with the skills they need to fill those jobs; and government that ensures not just that it’s acting as a convening body, but ensures that our national policies reflect these priorities. These three pillars working together drive us towards this outcome that we want, and it’s very important. So, I think today is a great way to kick this off. We have great partners on board already. We hope to attract more. I want to thank all of you for being a part of it. And I – the last thing I want to say about this is that we understand that for this to work, this is not a two-year project. This is not a two-and-a-half-year project. This is a project that will involve sustainment for the long term. Multiple American administrations are going to have to make this a priority, which is why it’s so important that you see evidence that, at the highest levels of our government, now and for the future, you have that commitment. And it’s why it’s exciting for us to have the Vice President here today to speak about it, because I think the evidence is not just the importance this administration gives it, but our acknowledgement that this is an issue that’s going to require long-term and sustained attention. This has to be an endeavor that goes on beyond the next two years. It has to go on for a generation. And I think having the Vice President here today with us is evidence of that commitment. And so now I want to introduce and welcome to the stage here at the Institute of Peace, a beautiful building that the State Department’s using a lot – and we thank you all for coming – the Vice President of the United States of America, JD Vance. (Applause.) title: Trump Administration Launches Foundry School to Build the Workforce Behind America’s Manufacturing Comeback
text: hide Trump Administration Launches Foundry School to Build the Workforce Behind America’s Manufacturing Comeback Fact Sheet Office of the Spokesperson September 3, 2026 Vice President J.D. Vance and Secretary Marco Rubio announced today the launch of Foundry School , a training program for entrepreneurs, engineers, technicians, and industrial leaders to rebuild American manufacturing. Under Secretary for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg hosted the event at the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace, joined by presidents and senior leaders from the eight universities working to deliver the Foundry School curriculum and chief executives and company presidents from manufacturing and technology companies. Putting American Workers First President Trump’s reindustrialization agenda has already brought trillions of dollars in industrial investment to American soil. Foundry School will focus on turning that investment into jobs. American manufacturers will need an estimated 3.8 million skilled workers by 2033 in semiconductors, defense, energy, and beyond. The State Department, working with Congress, plans to support the participation of Pax Silica economies in Foundry School and is working with Stanford University to develop the curriculum for U.S. and foreign participants. Foundry School will collaborate with Pax Silica economies to create opportunities for America and partners in industries critical to our nation’s economic security. A Historic Workforce Development Program Foundry School is anchored in a first-of-its-kind advanced manufacturing curriculum developed by Stanford University that also features keystone lectures provided by seven universities with which Stanford University has collaborated: Arizona State University, Georgia Institute of Technology, The Ohio State University, The Pennsylvania State University, the University of Kansas, Vanderbilt University, and Washington University in St. Louis. Across these eight campuses, the program will run 17 sessions, each taught by founders and CEOs from advanced manufacturing enterprises. These industry leaders will be drawn from the United States and Pax Silica participants, including the Republic of Korea, Japan, Taiwan, and India, covering everything it takes to build and run a world-class manufacturing enterprise. Cutting Edge Curriculum Foundry School is intended to close gaps in design and manufacturing capacity. The curriculum will unfold in two phases. Seven regional sessions, beginning in September 2026 and hosted by Arizona State University, Georgia Institute of Technology, The Ohio State University, The Pennsylvania State University, the University of Kansas, Vanderbilt University, and Washington University in St. Louis, will cover the fundamentals of modern factory design, materials and supply chains, assembly-line engineering, plant economics, regulation and permitting, and workforce development at scale. A ten-session core program hosted by Stanford University, beginning in January 2027, will build on that foundation with advanced manufacturing capabilities, including precision tooling, industrial automation, quality systems, new product introduction, digital manufacturing, capital equipment, energy, global site selection, and defense production, concluding with a capstone session on lessons from failed manufacturing ventures. Together, the 17 sessions form a one-of-a-kind curriculum. A Flagship Initiative of Pax Silica Foundry School is a flagship initiative of Pax Silica , the Trump Administration’s economic security partnership connecting governments, industry, and universities to strengthen the critical supply chains and industrial capabilities that underpin the AI economy. Foundry School connects students and workers directly with the companies building and operating advanced manufacturing facilities. For media inquiries, please submit a request . For further information for universities and companies, contact FoundrySchool@state.gov . title: Promoting Pacific Prosperity: U.S. Engagement at the Pacific Islands Forum
text: hide Promoting Pacific Prosperity: U.S. Engagement at the Pacific Islands Forum Media Note Office of the Spokesperson September 1, 2026 The United States is a Pacific nation and has long stood with our Pacific friends and neighbors to advance a free and open Indo-Pacific region. Our commitment to the security and prosperity of the Pacific Islands is steadfast, enduring, and a key pillar of our America First Foreign Policy. On September 1, at the Pacific Islands Forum Partners Dialogue in Palau, Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau announced over $150 million in U.S. support for Pacific Islands. He delivered this message directly to our partners, engaging with Pacific Islands leaders and ministers to reinforce the depth and durability of U.S. partnerships in the region and announcing new U.S.-funded projects and investments in the Pacific Islands that aim to deliver economic prosperity and security for Americans and Pacific Islanders. The United States’ continued participation in the Pacific Islands Forum reflects the importance we place on the Pacific Islands as a vital part of the Indo-Pacific region. When the Pacific Islands are stable, secure and prosperous, the United States is too. Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio’s leadership, we are prioritizing commercial diplomacy and reorienting our foreign assistance programs in the Pacific around championing U.S. enterprise and investments in enabling infrastructure that supports private sector-led economic growth. Ensuring Energy Security Regional Energy Security Initiative : Working with Congress, the Department intends to provide $60 million to help Pacific Islands countries address the ongoing global energy crisis, including expanding fuel storage capacity and supporting grid stability. Fuel Supply Infrastructure for Tonga : The U.S. Trade and Development Agency (USTDA), with funding from the U.S. Department of State, will strengthen fuel supply reliability and energy security through a feasibility study to upgrade Tonga’s port facilities, fuel storage capacity, pipeline infrastructure and market-oriented regulatory practices. Building Critical Infrastructure Palau Hospital Relocation: The United States, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea, along with Taiwan as a key partner of Palau, will support the development and operation of a new, modern hospital facility, subject to the outcomes of the project feasibility study, ensuring it meets the long-term health and infrastructure needs of the Palauan people. This partnership demonstrates our enduring commitment to Pacific partners and to the shared development principles that underpin a resilient and prosperous region. Upgrading Penrhyn (Omoka) Port: The U.S. Department of State, working with Congress and in partnership with New Zealand and the Cook Islands, intends to upgrade the Penrhyn atoll’s Omoka Port. This project builds on the Critical Minerals Framework the United States and the Cook Islands signed in February 2026 and will deliver safety and security benefits and expand transport links and economic opportunities for the Cook Islands and American people. Strengthening Transportation Linkages in the Marshall Islands: USTDA has approved funding for technical assistance for the Marshall Islands Ports Authority to help modernize the country’s two primary ports: Majuro and Ebeye. The project’s goals are to increase freight capacity, improve port efficiency, and strengthen supply chain reliability. USTDA has also approved funding for technical assistance to help modernize the Amata Kabua International Airport, including airfield and terminal facilities. The assistance will address anticipated growth and operational improvements over a 20-year horizon and facilitate aviation partnership opportunities for U.S. industry. Expanding Commercial Diplomacy Second Pacific Investment Summit: The inaugural U.S.-Pacific Islands Investment Summit at the East-West Center in Honolulu in February 2026 generated several successful economic opportunities and business deals for U.S. and Pacific Islands businesses across several sectors including infrastructure, critical minerals, supply chains, energy, tourism, food security, financial services, and the digital economy. To continue to foster U.S.-Pacific Islands private sector connections and investments, the United States intends to support a second summit to be held in early 2027. Promoting Trusted Digital Technology Data Center Infrastructure for Tonga: USTDA, with funding from the U.S. Department of State, is supporting a feasibility study to modernize Tonga’s national data center and network, enabling secure, resilient hosting for government systems and public services. The study advances a broader U.S. effort to build Tonga’s digital infrastructure on trusted American technology, alongside State Department support for secure cloud migration. Mobile Network Modernization for the Marshall Islands: USTDA, with funding from the U.S. Department of State, will provide technical assistance to support the modernization of the nationwide mobile network in the Republic of the Marshall Islands. The assistance will identify optimal technology options, financing pathways and implementation strategies for the Marshall Islands National Telecommunications Authority. Cloud Global Pacific Program: The U.S. Department of State plans to expand upon successful programming in Tonga and Palau to accelerate additional Pacific Island governments’ adoption of resilient cloud-based technologies. Adopting trusted cloud services expands the digital economy, creates opportunities for economic prosperity, strengthens cybersecurity, and increases operational continuity. Secure Telecom Regulation and Digital Transformation Programs in the Pacific Islands: S. Department’s Bureau of Cyberspace and Digital Policy (CDP) has funded a series of programs, coordinated by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Commercial Law Development Program (CLDP), to strengthen ICT regulatory capacity, expand digital infrastructure, and modernize regulatory and licensing models, including a PNG Secure ICT Investment Screening Workshop and Pacific Islands Telecom Regulator Workshop, and Study Tour. Additionally, CDP led the U.S.-Pacific Islands Digital Transformation Accelerator conference, held alongside the Pacific Islands Telecom Regulators’ Forum, generating 32 matchmaking sessions between U.S. technology companies and PIC governments, advancing potential leads for U.S. AI exports and digital sector investment. Advancing Law Enforcement Cooperation and Maritime Security U.S.-Pacific Islands Conference of Police Ministers (COPMIN): The United States and Palau will co-chair the inaugural U.S.-Pacific Islands Conference of Police Ministers (COPMIN). COPMIN will focus on maritime security, drug trafficking, and cybercrime, and illicit finance. Pacific Regional IUU Fishing Project : The U.S. Department of State, working with Congress, plans to provide $17 million to counter illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing in the Pacific Islands, focused on legal support to update national laws, policies, and regulations to align to regional IUU fishing strategic objectives, develop compliance officer capacity through certified training programs, and deploy new technologies to increase non-human monitoring capacity. Deepening Scientific and Technical Cooperation Seabed Mapping, Exploration, and Characterization : The U.S. Department of State, working with Congress, plans to provide support for seabed mapping, exploration, and characterization to inform Pacific Island government decision making on potential seabed minerals development within national jurisdiction and related national regulatory frameworks. Drinking Water Sampling Project : The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), in partnership with Taiwan, will work with Palau to conduct a comprehensive drinking water sampling project on the island’s drinking water sources and wells. The project will also provide training for Palau drinking water operators and environmental lab regulatory staff on proper sampling and logistical techniques. Expanding People to People Ties Peace Corps Letter of Intent to Return to Compact of Free Association Nations: The Peace Corps has signed a letter of intent to establish the North Pacific program with the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands, and the Republic of Palau. This step builds on decades of partnership: more than 4,400 Volunteers served in Micronesia and Palau between 1966 and 2018, and more than 140 served in the Marshall Islands from 1966 to 1996. The agency completed its re-opening of Peace Corps/Palau in July 2026. Tags Bureau of East Asian and Pacific Affairs Deputy Secretary of State Indo-Pacific Office of the Spokesperson Pacific Islands

title: Responding to the Murillo-Ortega Dictatorship’s Legislative Sham
text: hide Responding to the Murillo-Ortega Dictatorship’s Legislative Sham Press Statement Marco Rubio, Secretary of State September 2, 2026 Yesterday, Rosario Murillo and Daniel Ortega’s captive National Assembly eroded the fiction of Nicaragua’s democracy, again rewriting the nation’s constitution to entrench their illegitimate dynasty and indefinitely deprive Nicaraguans of free and fair elections. Dictatorships that deny the unalienable rights of their citizens should not enjoy the same economic or political benefits as governments committed to defending hemispheric peace and security. The United States urges international partners to immediately stop business as usual operations with this brutal dictatorship. Murillo and Ortega’s war on democracy threatens our hemisphere’s stability and prosperity. The Trump Administration remains committed to identifying and implementing actions to address the Murillo-Ortega’s violations of human rights, including at forums like the Organization of American States. We stand in support of Nicaraguans’ right to decide their country’s future. title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio with Brian Kilmeade on The Brian Kilmeade Show
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio with Brian Kilmeade on The Brian Kilmeade Show Interview Marco Rubio, Secretary of State Via Teleconference September 2, 2026 QUESTION: All right, Mr. Secretary, Marco Rubio, thanks so much for joining us – and National Security Advisor. I understand the Iranians are, on the recipient of American attacks. In fact, the President put on Truth Social – and I’ll read some of it: The U.S., as we speak, is striking Iran near the strait. The strikes are large and powerful, and the retaliation for Iran’s failed attempt at adding sea mines to the strait, which currently has no mines and the Iranians shooting eight missiles at us, all successfully knocked down. If the failed nation of Iran retaliates for the very justified attack, they’ll be hit again as much harder at a higher level. Mr. Secretary, where do you think we’re at with this Iran confrontation, six months in? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, first of all, I’ll remind everybody that, at the end, the core and central issue here is the following: Iran will never be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon, certainly not as long as President Trump is in office. So that’s first and foremost. With regards to the Strait of Hormuz, while our primary vehicle by which we are preventing them from getting a nuclear weapon and inflicting the price and a cost on them is economic, we always reserve the right to defend the interests – our interests in the region. Iran has continued to fire on shipping, continued to fire on commercial shipping in the straits. They’re losing control of the straits; they’ve lost control of the straits. Their mines were – they put a bunch of mines in there. We were able to successfully destroy those mines, and so the shipping lanes are now even broader. But they keep shooting at things, and they keep shooting at ships. So we will continue to target those things that pose an imminent threat to our forces and to global shipping in the straits. The straits will remain open, and they will not be under Iranian control. And that’s what you’re seeing the President carrying out right now. QUESTION: Understood. And also from their perspective – I understand they speak from many different areas – the IRGC has a spokesperson, the parliament has a spokesperson, and they also have a president who came out and essentially said we’d like to go back to the MOU. What does Secretary of State Marco Rubio say about that? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, look, I mean, that ship, in many ways, has sailed – no pun intended with regards to the straits – because, if you think about it, as a moment – I mean, at the core issue here is they’re never going to have a nuclear weapon. I have to remind people of that continuously. This is all about the fact that they want to possess a nuclear weapon and threaten the world with it, and we’ll never allow that to happen. And as long as they continue to endeavor or claim to want one, they’re going to pay a price for it, and that price is going to be primarily economic. But we reserve the right, as we said, to take military action when necessary – not just to protect ourselves but to prevent them from being able to threaten others as well. So as far as the differences in their system, here’s the bottom line – their economy’s a disaster. It was a disaster before all of this, right, because they – if you think about it, Iran – every penny they get, be it through sanctions relief or whatever – every penny they get, they don’t spend it on the Iranian people. They don’t spend that money on their country. They use that money to fund Hizballah and Hamas and terrorist organizations and militias in Iraq to threaten us and threaten the world. If they spent a fraction, just half the money that they’re spending on these militias – if they spent it on their own people, the Iranian people would be better off. So they’re going to continue to feel the squeeze, because understand that this is not just about punishing Iran, the Iranian regime. It’s about preventing them from having access to money that will then be used to sponsor terrorism, which is what they’ve always done. They want money for two things – to sponsor terrorism and ultimately to have a nuclear weapon. And we can’t allow that to happen. QUESTION: We saw president – Prime Minister Modi meet with the Iranian president and Iranian officials, and it essentially looked like they’re setting up some type of trade deal. Pakistan two weeks before. What’s your message for those countries? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t think there’s a trade deal between India and Iran. Obviously, there are – countries all develop their own foreign policy, and many countries around the world talk to the Iranian regime. I mean, we’ve met with elements of the Iranian regime as well, in terms of some of these discussions that have occurred and there’s been contact with them. I think what ultimately happens though is – and the President’s been very clear – is no country should be helping Iran evade sanctions. No country should be out there helping them create mechanisms by which they can generate revenue that they will then use to sponsor terrorism and try to build a nuclear weapon. And if countries decide to do that, then we’re going to have to sanction them too. QUESTION: So Vladimir Putin says this to Iran: During this difficult time, we’re trying to provide you with the assistance you need. We have discussed this with you and are supplying you with the necessary goods. We always thought they were giving – it seems as though they’re giving satellite coordinates to help kill our people, but now we have the Russians saying directly we’re helping you out. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. Well, in the case, unfortunately, of Iran, we’re not aligned with the Russians and the Russian system in terms of their view of the situation. Obviously, Russia has their own hands full with Ukraine and that effort there. But I’ve said this before, and I’ll say it again: Nothing that anyone is providing Iran is in any way impeding our ability to act as necessary to protect the United States. That said, it is clear that, in the case of what Iran is doing, we are not necessarily fully aligned with the Russian position on it, but Russia’s got – and Putin’s got his own set of problems that I think take up the majority of his time and focus, which is the war in – with Ukraine, and frankly the impacts that these Ukrainian strikes are having on the Russian economy in combination with sanctions. QUESTION: I’m talking to Secretary Rubio, obviously. Mr. Secretary, appreciate your time. So when you talk about John Ratcliffe, he had 72-hour mission, six hours on the ground in Russia. We don’t know exactly what he discussed, but I imagine it was important. Some have said it was a proposal to have a trilateral meeting between President Trump, President Zelenskyy, and President Putin, as well as warning them – letting them know the reality on the ground is you’re not doing very well. Is there anything you could share with the country about what that meeting was about? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, I’ve seen those reports, and I don’t know where those are coming from, because nobody who has any knowledge of that meeting is – it’s a very small handful of people, and none of them have talked to the press. So this is stuff they’re getting secondhand and reporting on, and – but let me just say that trip was primarily a routine one. It is not unprecedented. Despite whatever differences you may have geopolitically, the United States does have to be able to communicate with Russia from a very practical perspective. They are – they have the largest, second-largest nuclear stockpile in the world. The United States has to be able to communicate with them. I have met with the foreign minister; we talk to their foreign ministry. We’re engaged with them in that regard. And I think, for a long period of time, there’s been exchanges between our respective intelligence communities, including our Department of War in deconfliction and things of this nature. This has always existed. So his visit there was largely routine in that sense of just establishing and continue to build these intel-to-intel communication channels. Because they’re – those things can prove useful in a time of crisis or conflict. I mean, this is not unusual; it’s occurred under other administrations as well. And – but – they’re really – it wasn’t part of any sort of broader initiative, other than continuing to establish those intel-to-intel channels that can prove useful in any particular contingency or crisis situation. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, I also know that President Zelenskyy appreciates the support of the President now, but he says specifically they would just need Patriots, 5 percent more Patriots. I know there’s only a finite number available. Is there a plan in place to help them with missile defense leading into the winter? SECRETARY RUBIO: I mean, we’ve provided that in the past. And obviously, as you know, the whole world is asking for more air interceptors. It’s become the number-one defense need on the planet – not just for Ukraine, but on the planet. Countries in the Middle East want it. I know Iran wishes they had interceptors, which they don’t, which is why we’re able to act the way we do and do some of the things we have, because those things were wiped out by us. But multiple countries around the world – look, it’s just a question of availability. And obviously, I have to remind people the United States has needs. Like, we have our own defense needs; we have our own defense requirements. And before we can help others, we have to make sure that our stockpiles are always sufficient. I think there’s a lot that’s been reported inaccurately about what U.S. stockpiles are – I think dangerously, too, because I think in some ways our adversaries read that stuff and think it’s true, and they try to test us, and it could lead to conflict. But the U.S. I think, nonetheless – oh, and this is not new now; this has always been the case. We have minimum requirements of our own, and those always have to be met before we can provide others. As the President’s been clear, I mean, we’ve provided more assistance to Ukraine over the last few years than anybody else has, and we continue to provide them assistance within the limits of our own availability and capability. We always have to look out for America first. QUESTION: Are you against giving them the licenses to make their own? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, that’s being negotiated as we speak. And as I said, again – but that is not an immediate solution. I mean, ramping up production, even if you have a license, is something that takes multiple years to build these factories. I mean, these are highly sophisticated weaponry. So that’s being negotiated now. That may come to fruition, but it really won’t solve the short-term challenge that they’re pointing to. QUESTION: Ukraine wants to help us with their drone technology and the unbelievable success they had against Russia. Have we been reluctant to accept their offer to use some of that incredible drone technology? SECRETARY RUBIO: No, look, I think if it’s a deal that makes – no, if there’s a deal that makes sense for the United States, I think we’re pursuing those, and we’re negotiating those, and those are all a work in progress. I don’t have an announcement on it today, but we’re always looking for ways to strengthen our own defenses. And if someone has an ability to partner with us and create that, we’d certainly be open to it. But again, these are long-term projects; these are not the kinds of things that you would see come online immediately. QUESTION: When you talk about the Lindsey Graham bill – I guess they’re calling it now – which would give the massive sanctions, it got 85 votes in the Senate – you used to be in the Senate; nothing gets 85 votes anymore – that said give secondary sanctions to anybody dealing with Russia, which would include China, Turkey, South Africa, Pakistan, whoever’s doing it, they would be susceptible to these secondary sanctions. Would you encourage the House to pass this? Because right now, Democrats are holding it up more than even Republicans. Would you like to see that on the President’s desk? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, look, I mean, it gives the President the authority to do these things. It gives him more tools in the toolbox. Now, he can do a lot of it without the bill, but obviously the Democrats in the House are not apparently in a mood to provide the President any additional legal powers and to impose tariffs and other penalties. But I think it would be valuable for the President to have these tools available to him, and then he can decide if and when to use them appropriately, given changing circumstances. So as we said, the White House was supportive of it passing in the Senate, and we would see that the House hopefully take it up. But right now, the opposition to it, as you said, is coming from Democrats that just don’t want to pass a bill that gives the President more authority, even though they claim to be supportive of Ukraine. QUESTION: So when we come – so let’s just fast forward to Canadian talks. I never thought that we’d be talking about Canada and a rift between our two countries, but it looks as though the trade talks have broken off. September 8th, they’re going to put in a whole bunch of tariffs on us. We’re going to hit them at the beginning of 2027. Is there anything you can do as Secretary of State to try to get these back on track? And can you tell the country what happened between two weeks ago – because it looked like we had a deal Friday afternoon and we had – it all broke apart Friday night. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, so our Trade Representative, Jamieson Greer, leads those talks on – so he’s probably the right person to ask in better detail about the prospects moving forward. Suffice it to say, though, that we did believe, at some point two weeks ago, that we were very close to a deal. In fact, everybody assumed one was about to happen because the terms had been agreed to. And then there was a change in the Canadian position at the last second that sort of unraveled it all. So obviously, the hope is that we can get back to that original arrangement because we thought it was a good arrangement and a fair arrangement for both countries, but let’s see what happens. I can’t really prognosticate how it plays forward. I think some of that is tied into some domestic Canadian politics as well and some of the things going on over there. So I don’t want to opine too much on it other than to say that we thought we had a really good deal, a very fair deal. We were on the verge of executing on it and then there was a change at the last minute in the Canadian position. So it either will happen, and if it doesn’t, then there’ll be consequences for it, unfortunately. But hopefully we can get back to that. QUESTION: You’re not too far from when you were in politics, and you know that Michigan and Maine will probably make or break the Senate for either party. Does it concern you at all that the – that Leader Carney has reached out to governors to kind of say, this is my point of view when it comes to the trade deal, almost bypassing the federal government? And do you think that the liberal leader of Canada is trying to make sure that the Republican President does not have a successful midterm election? SECRETARY RUBIO: I don’t — QUESTION: Do you think politics is playing into this? SECRETARY RUBIO: It might be, but I don’t think it has any impact ultimately. I mean, you can – you can’t do a trade deal with a governor. If he wants a trade deal and they want a trade deal with the United States, there’s a good deal on the table. They should have taken it when it was available. And maybe they’ll get back to it, but in the end, they really can’t circumvent President Trump. I mean, he holds all the cards here on this — QUESTION: Right. SECRETARY RUBIO: — because he’s the President, and these are deals with our – with the federal government, not with state governments. So — QUESTION: So Venezuela has been an unbelievable success. We know that Delcy Rodríguez, the interim leader of that country, worked out a tremendous oil deal between our two countries. They’re gradually releasing political prisoners. But this is what Ted Cruz said on Sunday that he wants to see happen in Venezuela: SENATOR CRUZ: There need to be democratic, free elections in Venezuela. Delcy Rodríguez was Nicolás Maduro’s vice president. Maduro was illegitimate. He was a Marxist. He had seized power contrary to the will of the voters. And from the beginning, I have been urging – and I believe the administration is working towards this – that there should be free and fair elections. QUESTION: Your thoughts to Senator Ted Cruz and others? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: How close are elections? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t – yeah, I don’t know what the disagreement is. I mean, I don’t think there is one. I mean, we’ve been – worked with – we’ve been very clear about the three-step process involved here. The first was stabilization. We have a country that, after 20 years of chavismo and Marxism, was deeply broken and corrupt. And the first thing we had to avoid is civil war or mass migration or systemic collapse of the country because that wouldn’t have been good for the Venezuelan people, wouldn’t have been good for anybody. And we’ve largely achieved that despite a devastating earthquake that required us to step in and do a bunch of stuff to help them because they had – for all those years of chavismo had not invested at all in some of the capabilities that governments basically need because the money had been stolen. The second is a recovery phase, which is you have to rebuild the economy and rebuild it in a way that’s credible, that’s legitimate. And the third is the democratic transition. And these things – when I say third, it’s not in sequence. I mean, you can have the democratic transition happening at the same time. But if you think about it, what do we want from a democratic transition? We don’t just want there to be an election. Election is important, but we want to make sure that it leads to a republic, to an enduring republic that has elections on a regular basis for the foreseeable future. We don’t – what we don’t want to see is a country that has an election and then the leader takes over a catastrophe, the country’s in tailspin, and it all falls apart. So we are engaged in that now. I mean, the talks are happening between the – the last democratically legitimate National Assembly in Venezuela was the 2015 National Assembly. And through our facilitation, they have begun talks with the interim government towards that goal of the democratically elected – having democratic elections. But democratic elections are more than just about having an election because you could have an election tomorrow; we’d still be using the Chávez machines and the Chávez electoral committee, and it would not be credible. All those things have to be transformed; all of that has to be changed. You need a free press. You need the time and space for political parties who are going to run in those elections to organize themselves. A lot of the most prominent leaders in Venezuela’s opposition still live abroad. They need the opportunity to return to the country and organize themselves to run for office. All of that remains a priority of this administration, and it’s something we’re working towards; and in fact, the next phase of these talks – these transitional talks – will happen here in about 10 days, again facilitated by us. So we remain very committed to that prospect, and ultimately that is where this project needs to wind up. What we don’t want to see is something like what happened in Nicaragua 25 years ago, where they had an election but, four years later, the Sandinistas were back in power. So you have to have – this is a holistic process that has to take place, and it’s important. And we’re nine months into this. It’s not going to take as long as it took in Eastern Europe, but it took Eastern Europe four to five years to fully transition. We can do it much faster here; we’re pushing very hard on it. We need that to happen. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, I see the unbelievable success in Central and South America as they begin to transition towards more representative governments, from Argentina to Bolivia, to what we’re seeing now in Venezuela, and it seems like Cuba is teetering. How much longer do you expect this Cuban Government to stay in power? And how important would it be for the United States interests for that to become a representative government, a democratic government? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, first of all, Cuba is a failed state right now, and it’s not because of us. People say it’s because of us; it’s not. Cuba was getting free oil from Maduro. Maduro was literally stealing the oil of the people of Venezuela and giving it for free to Cuba. Cuba would take that oil – and they weren’t using it to benefit the Cuban people; they were selling the majority of that oil for cash, and that cash was going into their pockets. That’s no longer happening. That’s the number one thing that’s happened here, is they’re no longer stealing the oil of Venezuela and getting it for free. And so – so that really is the fundamental challenge they face in terms of – but their energy sector. You see these blackouts in Cuba. These blackouts are not new; they’ve been having blackouts for five or seven years. You know why? Because their system doesn’t function; it doesn’t work. They have equipment from the 1940s and ’50s, and they haven’t re-upped it or invested in it at all, because the economic model doesn’t work. So I think the goal is that Cuba – the only solution and answer to Cuba – and we’re prepared to play a productive role in this – is to place itself on an irreversible path towards becoming a normal functioning state that eventually, of course, also is a democratic one as well. That’s the future of Venezuela, and by – future of Cuba. And by the way, U.S. policy towards Cuba, unlike U.S. policy towards Venezuela or other countries – U.S. policy towards Cuba is codified. It’s in statute; there’s a law. And that law regulates what we can and cannot do with Cuba, and it makes very clear that ultimately, normalization between our countries cannot fully happen – under that law passed by Congress over 20-something years ago – cannot happen unless there’s a functioning democracy, or at least steps towards a functioning democracy. So in many ways, when it comes to Cuba policy, it’s governed not simply by the desires of an administration; it’s governed by law that’s sitting on our books. QUESTION: Are you concerned at all – before I let you go, and I know you’ve got to run to do 20 million things for your many jobs – are you concerned at all about the transition in the Pentagon, with – you no longer have a secretary of the Army; there’s been no replacement for Randy George as – as – I think he was chief of staff of the Army. Are you concerned at all about the churn, with no more Chris Donahu either; he was the head of European Command. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, look. I mean, first of all, these combatant commands rotate out quite often. There’ll be some that are in place now that will – are soon about to term out. So I think Pete’s doing a great job at the Pentagon and the Department of War. In every administration, there’s always transitions. There are people coming and going for a variety of different reasons. Many people who sign up for work in the public sector and in government do so for a defined period of time with the understanding that they can do it for two years, or they can do it for a year and a half, or they can do it for three years. So it’s not abnormal. This – every administration has turnover. And obviously, look, when you’re trying to systemically reorganize an agency, like one as big and as large as the Pentagon is, there are going to have to be some changes made, which is one of the things – some of the things that Pete Hegseth has done. But I think Pete’s doing a great job. QUESTION: Do you see yourself taking more of a leadership role in Ukraine with the Hamas transition and now, of course, with Iran? A more direct — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, yeah, look. I mean, we’re — QUESTION: — because they seem to be gummed up? SECRETARY RUBIO: Just by the nature of the position that I’m in, both Secretary of State with the Department of State, which has jurisdiction and not just jurisdiction but actually has to do things, and also the National Security Advisor that works directly for the President from the White House, there is – none of these things involve – they’re all involved as part of a team effort. We have – we’ve built teams around all of these things, so we have people that are designed who are – I’m sorry, whose directive is to negotiate peace agreements. And that’s Steve Witkoff, and now Jared Kushner is involved in that, and these are people that dedicate themselves 100 percent of the time to sort of negotiating peace agreements. But obviously all of this happens to the dynamic, and primarily in my role as National Security Advisor is to coordinate the interagency, because none of these issues stand on their own. For example, Iran. You look at Iran as an example. Iran has a component that involves Treasury. It has a component that involves the Department of Energy. It has a component that involves the Department of State. It obviously has a component that involves the Department of War. It also involves the policy considerations of the White House. And the job of the National Security Council, which I chair, is to coordinate all of these agencies to make sure that we’re all pulling and pushing in the same direction and taking what the President is ordering and executing it. That’s our job, and that will continue to be our job whether it’s Russia-Ukraine, whether it’s Iran, whether it’s the Western Hemisphere, whether it’s any part of the world. QUESTION: What worries you the most? SECRETARY RUBIO: What worries me the most about the world? QUESTION: About all those conflicts I just brought up between Cuba, Ukraine, Iran, Hamas — SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, I mean these are all very – these are all great challenges. And then there’s the challenges that are unforeseen, that come up from time to time, that you try to get ahead of but you can’t always do. Look, the world remains what it is: a risky place. I think the world is going through a period of transition, and both economic transition and geopolitical transition. And I think – I don’t know if it’s a worry, but I think the one thing that we have to understand is that a lot of these problems that are going on in the world don’t have simple answers and sometimes don’t have perfect answers. Many times when it comes to foreign affairs and geopolitics, you’re not choosing between a perfect answer and a bad answer; you’re choosing between two less-than-ideal approaches, and you’re trying to figure out which one of the two is least harmful to the interests of the United States. So I don’t know if it’s a worry, but I think the one thing I always focus on every single day is we have to understand that we cannot just deal with the immediate – like, what’s right in front of us. That has to be dealt with of course, but you also have to be thinking long term. What’s the world going to look like in two years, five years, even 10 years from now? And there are things you have to do now to either prevent bad things from happening down the road, or to get ahead of those things before they happen. And so I wouldn’t call it a worry, but I would call it a focus of this administration is not simply to deal with what’s right in front of us, but also to deal with what will be in front of us at some point in the future, and make sure that our national interests are being protected. So in the case of, like, just a perfect example is this arrangement in Venezuela with the oil. Obviously it will have some short-term benefits, but it also ensures that the United States – not China, not Russia, not Iran – will have a position, a position that – with regards to the largest oil producer in our hemisphere as a hedge against a future conflict or crisis that maybe is unforeseen right now but could threaten our energy security long term. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, with all that on your mind I know you have a lot to do today. Thank you so much for your quality time, too. We appreciate it. SECRETARY RUBIO: Of course. Thank you.
