Like, he’s not – he just – he tells – he’s a great narrator. And he’s got incredible – people don’t realize, like, he’s been a public figure for almost half a century. Like, he has – he met a lot of people, and he’s gotten to know a lot of people over the years. And so he has great stories going back to, like, celebrities in the ’80s and people he interacted with and people he was around. So I don’t know of one in particular that stands out, but I’m fascinated by these stories because some of these are stories that go – I mean, he knew Michael Jackson. He knew – he knew everybody. He knew everybody at some point or another. He had interacted with everybody. He’s just got great stories. If you ask him about somebody, he’ll go back and tell you about them. And it’s a pretty amazing life he’s lived. QUESTION: When he approached you to be secretary of state, is that something you were seeking or did that just happen? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, I don’t know if “approach” is the right term. He just basically called me and told me, you’re going to be the secretary of state. (Laughter.) It wasn’t presented as, like, an option – (a) you can stay in the Senate, or (b) you can — QUESTION: And you said okay. Did you think about it? SECRETARY RUBIO: Not really. I mean, I think I’m – there had been some sense that that – something like that could happen. But it was the middle of the campaign and I wasn’t going to raise it, and he wasn’t going to talk about it. But I think it was maybe, like, 48 hours after – or maybe 72 hours – it wasn’t long after the election. He just basically called me and said, hey, this is what – I think he had even already Truth-posted it, and then he told me about it. So it was – (laughter) – and I was happy to do it, and I was honored to do it. I’m not saying that. I’m just saying it generally wasn’t presented as, like, “Hey, would you be interested in…” It was more like, “Hey, you’re going to be,” and I said okay, here we go. QUESTION: You’ve been one of the toughest voices on Cuba forever. We captured Maduro out of Venezuela. Is Cuba next? SECRETARY RUBIO: I think Cuba – I am confident that Cuba, by the time this administration’s over, before this administration ends, will be on an irreversible path towards a much different future. Obviously, like anything else, especially something like this, I always tell people, like, you can’t have something in place for 70 years, it grows roots, and then think overnight you’re just going to rip out the whole thing and put something brand-new into the ground. There’s a transition that has to happen and a process to get there. Eastern Europe is instructive of that. You saw it took countries in Eastern Europe three to five years to truly become what we know them to be today. Poland is probably the best example. So I think Cuba will be on that path, well along that path. It has to be. But certainly under this administration, given the priority it’s given Cuba, I – I – like, you never guarantee anything, but it’s certainly a priority for us because it’s in our national interest. I remind people, at the end of the day, like, I work for the United States of America. I care about Cuba, obviously I have a personal connection to it, but I don’t work for Cuba; I work for the United States. And I believe it’s in the national interest of our country to have a Cuba that’s safe and stable and aligned with the U.S. – the same feeling I have about Venezuela as well. QUESTION: When the Maduro raid happened, what was it like leading up to that? What was he like? Was he nervous? What was the vibes? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, she didn’t really know. She knew something was up, but she didn’t know. MRS RUBIO: Yeah, I knew something was going on just based on, I mean, he was constantly in and out; we didn’t do anything during the holidays. So I knew something was going on, but I didn’t know exactly what it was. QUESTION: When there’s big things going on in the world, can you often tell based on how his demeanor changes, or is he pretty calm, cool, and collected? MRS RUBIO: I don’t know. That’s a good question. I think I just see him busier. I just see him more on the phone. He’s just – he’s thinking. But he’s – I would say he’s cool and collected. I mean, I – that’s – I wouldn’t say he isn’t, but — QUESTION: You said to Lara Trump if you had a day off that you would watch football all day. SECRETARY RUBIO: I answered the question completely wrong. QUESTION: (Laughter.) Why? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, first of all, the true – the right answer is I would spend it with my wife going wherever she wants to go. (Laughter.) MRS RUBIO: Oh, yeah, okay. What a beautiful answer. SECRETARY RUBIO: But the true answer is – and I – here’s where I messed up that answer, okay? Because here’s the thing: The day would actually start much earlier. The greatest show on television today in America is College GameDay. Great show. Starts around 10 or 11, and that leads into noon, and then the noon game, and then there’s a 3:30 game, and then there’s a – so I messed – and the ideal – like, this is a crazy weekend; it would never happen. So I’m just putting this out there. But you could start at 10:00 a.m. on Saturday, run the whole college football day, sleep for a few hours, then you wake up and then you’re into NFL GameDay, then you’ve got the 1 o’clock game, the 4 o’clock game, the NBC game that night. That is an incredible weekend, in my opinion, in my view. Obviously, I don’t believe that will ever – I will ever achieve this; certainly not in the next two and a half years or what have you. But – and your audience probably doesn’t care anything about what I just said, but I’m just telling you that that would be a crazy day. But that’s never going to happen. Right? Maybe? MRS RUBIO: Well, you never know. SECRETARY RUBIO: You never know. QUESTION: Would you be okay with him watching that much football, or do you sit with him and watch the football, or are you off doing something else? SECRETARY RUBIO: No, she doesn’t watch. MRS RUBIO: No, no. I don’t. I mean, I’ll sit and watch some, but no. SECRETARY RUBIO: She’ll watch a game if my son is in the game. MRS RUBIO: Exactly. SECRETARY RUBIO: The one that’s at Florida. MRS RUBIO: Exactly. SECRETARY RUBIO: Or – that’s about it, actually. (Laughter.) That’s about it. MRS RUBIO: No, no, I probably would go and do some activities. QUESTION: How long did it take for you to figure out the State Department? SECRETARY RUBIO: Figure out the State Department? QUESTION: Yeah. Like, navigate it, figure it all out, unpack it all. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I think that’s still a learning process. I mean, along the way we’ve also done a – what I think was a very important reorganization of it, to bring it back more to its core principles. I think we did a lot of things that previous secretaries of state – many of whom will never admit it – wish they could have done in terms of, like, bringing foreign aid together with foreign policy so that they’re both pushing in the same direction. QUESTION: Did any of your predecessors give you advice coming into the job? SECRETARY RUBIO: A few. I mean, I don’t know “advice” is the right term; I think they gave me their impressions. But I think so much of what we do here is dependent on the times in which you live. If you were secretary of state in the middle of the Cold War, or secretary of state post-9/11, that’s a very different world from what we’re facing right now. So I think there’s some things they can give you advice on in terms of, like, how they managed their schedule and how – but ultimately the secretary of state works for the president. And so a lot of what you do in this job, and what this place does, should be geared and aligned and built around what the president – who the president is. And so a – a Department of State under President Trump is – should look different than it looks under the next president, what it’s going to look like under the next president, or previous presidents. It should be a reflection of the foreign policy direction that the current president wants to take it. QUESTION: You’ve been married for nearly three decades. What’s the secret to a happy marriage? MRS RUBIO: You answer the question. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t know that there’s a secret. There’s no secret. QUESTION: No, Jeanette smiled first. SECRETARY RUBIO: No, there’s no secret. I mean, it’s no – there’s no secret to it. It’s — MRS RUBIO: You have to have a friendship. I would start at that. You have – I would just say it starts with your faith, for me, and that’s a very important thing, and I think for Marco too, right? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. MRS RUBIO: And then — SECRETARY RUBIO: Compliance, for the husband. (Laughter.) MRS RUBIO: No, please. (Laughter.) I would say, truly, just have a friendship. I mean, we’ve known each other for so long. And we have to – you give and take. You have to have a give and take. QUESTION: Who’s more likely to apologize first after an argument? SECRETARY RUBIO: Oh, me, big-time. MRS RUBIO: (Laughter.) Oh, please. That’s not true. SECRETARY RUBIO: Are you kidding me? But I’ll say almost anything to move past it, whatever it was. Like, I – she has great memory and stuff, and I don’t. So for example, like – MRS RUBIO: (Laughter.) That is not true. SECRETARY RUBIO: — she can recall something that happened in 1999; on September of ’99, do you remember when you said or did this? And I’m like, no, I – actually I don’t remember this. And so she has an incredible sort of catalogue of – (laughter) – grievances that she’s able to use at appropriate times. As I, on the other hand, I – my preference is generally to move on from things quickly. Like, you deal with it off – you get mad, you get whatever, and then you just move quickly on it. So – but I don’t know. I mean, look, you asked that question about marriage. Marriage is not a – unfortunately people watch a lot of movies and stuff, and they think that marriage is about, oh, just two people that are always happy and always – I mean, it’s life. You make — MRS RUBIO: Right. SECRETARY RUBIO: You entered into a partnership to share life, and life is hard. There’s ups, there’s downs, there’s good days, there’s bad days, there’s great moments, there’s difficult moments, there’s disagreement. All of that is – so it takes, for lack of a better term, maybe it’s cliche-ish, but it really is a commitment to say, okay — MRS RUBIO: It’s a commitment. SECRETARY RUBIO: — we’ve agreed to live life and share life together, not just because you care about one another, but because of the commitment we’ve made to one another. And then you have to sort of ride that through. And there – a lot of times, unfortunately, I think people have been given this idealistic view that there – it’ll always be – every day will be phenomenal. And that’s just not true. QUESTION: What’s one habit the other person does that drives you absolutely insane, but you’ve just accepted it will never change? SECRETARY RUBIO: Oh, the sleep thing is the remaining irritant. I could be far more productive, believe it or not, had I not had the — MRS RUBIO: Yes, we have different sleeping patterns. SECRETARY RUBIO: But we have from the very beginning. MRS RUBIO: He likes to go to sleep early. I’m more of a late owl. SECRETARY RUBIO: In the early days of our marriage, okay, back in the day when they didn’t have some of the things you have now, she loved to watch – I wanted to go to sleep early because I like to wake up early. MRS RUBIO: By 8 o’clock. I mean, as early as possible. SECRETARY RUBIO: It depends. Because I used to get up, like, at 4:00 a.m. So yeah, this is a reasonable thing. And — MRS RUBIO: At 8 o’clock in the morning. And I’m like, who goes to sleep that early? So – SECRETARY RUBIO: All right, so we – her compromise was she bought these earphones. I’m talking about these big earphones that were plugged into the TV so she could — MRS RUBIO: (Laughter.) No, I didn’t buy them. He bought them. He – I never bought them. You bought them for me. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yes, okay, either way, we had these earphones – but I’m talking about the earphones so she could hear the audio, but the TV was still glowing. So the light would keep you up. MRS RUBIO: Exactly. So nothing was going to work. SECRETARY RUBIO: So then I bought – no, no, no – so then I bought those things you put around your eyes, and now I felt like – now it’s even worse, because now I felt like I was a hostage. (Laughter.) It’s like oh, this guy, he’s been blindfolded while he’s trying to sleep. And it doesn’t stay on. As soon as you turn, the thing’s coming off. You’ve got the things sideways on your face. MRS RUBIO: (Laughter.) It’s true. It’s true. It’s true. SECRETARY RUBIO: So we struggled – from the very beginning, that has been the one consistent irritant is — MRS RUBIO: It’s been a problem. It’s a problem in our home, exactly. It’s — SECRETARY RUBIO: I need to be asleep by a certain time so that I can wake up by a certain time. I don’t need 12 hours of sleep, but I need sleep. MRS RUBIO: No, yeah, he’s — SECRETARY RUBIO: She, on the other hand, can go to sleep in 30 seconds in any setting or scenario, and so that difference is deeply problematic. MRS RUBIO: And I’m fine – I can wake up three hours later and I’m fine. QUESTION: You don’t complain that you’re tired all day? MRS RUBIO: No, I don’t. I just don’t think about it. I just keep going. Yeah. He’s — QUESTION: What’s one thing you disagree with Marco on? MRS RUBIO: Oh, my gosh. SECRETARY RUBIO: One? (Laughter.) That’s for episode two. (Laughter.) MRS RUBIO: Oh, my gosh. Let me see. Let’s see. Just about some of the stuff he stresses on. I think — SECRETARY RUBIO: Like war and peace, for example? (Laughter.) MRS RUBIO: No, I’m talking about a personal level. I’m not talking about — SECRETARY RUBIO: Oh. MRS RUBIO: — when it comes to the world. I mean, just things. I mean, everything has to be like — SECRETARY RUBIO: Scheduled. MRS RUBIO: Everything has to be scheduled. See, I’m not always scheduled about everything. So I think that’s where we sometimes have — SECRETARY RUBIO: She’s more spontaneous. MRS RUBIO: I’m very spontaneous. SECRETARY RUBIO: And some things are great about spontaneity and some things are not. Like, for example, like, flights. (Laughter.) You can’t be spontaneous about a flight, right? There’s a commercial flight, it takes off at 10:05, and it’s — MRS RUBIO: No, but three hours – three hours prior, he’s already stressing. SECRETARY RUBIO: Because I’m preparing — MRS RUBIO: We’re not going to make it on time. We’re not going to be able to go. SECRETARY RUBIO: No. MRS RUBIO: Yes, you do. Absolutely that’s how you get. SECRETARY RUBIO: I’m preparing for all sorts of contingencies. MRS RUBIO: No, he’s thinking about the worst – the worst-case scenario. See, I don’t think about the worst-case scenario. SECRETARY RUBIO: If you’re prepared for the worst-case scenario in life, nothing will ever surprise you. MRS RUBIO: See, and I think, my gosh, and you live always frustrated. SECRETARY RUBIO: I mean, you just ask people – you go to the airport, and let’s say there’s a TSA meltdown, like that day they decide, oh, we’re not doing pre-check today, because it happens in these airports. MRS RUBIO: Have we ever missed a flight? SECRETARY RUBIO: No, because I’m – (laughter) — MRS RUBIO: That’s not true. Okay, either – have I ever missed a flight? No, I haven’t. SECRETARY RUBIO: No, you haven’t missed a flight, but you’ve gotten close. MRS RUBIO: No. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yes, close – a couple instances where it’s gotten close. MRS RUBIO: The bottom line, I’ve never missed a flight. So there you go. QUESTION: Do you miss driving? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, I do. QUESTION: Does that force you to be more scheduled now? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, I didn’t used to – I mean, I’m not – she loves to drive. I’m not a driving lover. MRS RUBIO: I am a driver. I love to drive. SECRETARY RUBIO: Like, I don’t – I’m not anti-driving, but I’m like a – but now I do. Like I – there are – not the driving like the daily driving, like the long – like a three-hour road trip somewhere, that you just get in your car – you rent a car because you’re going somewhere — QUESTION: Like Miami to Gainesville? SECRETARY RUBIO: Absolutely. I miss that so much. I would get in – like my son’s first year at the University of Florida, when I would go to some of the games, like, and she would – she couldn’t go because something was going on with my other son in Miami or whatever, I would get in the car, rent a car, take off driving. You put on XM radio, College Game Day on there. MRS RUBIO: Oh, my gosh. SECRETARY RUBIO: So you could hear the whole thing for five hours, no interruptions, nobody can stop you. And you’re driving, you’re listening to that, you pull in — QUESTION: Nobody can stop you? MRS RUBIO: So there you go, he would get his – he would get his whole day of football. SECRETARY RUBIO: You check into the hotel, you’re ready for game day, you go to game day, you come back, and then all the drive back the next day, you’re listening to the NFL stuff before it’s gearing up on XM. So I miss that. I miss those kinds of things, yeah. QUESTION: What’s the funniest parenting fail you’ve ever had? SECRETARY RUBIO: Parenting fail? QUESTION: Yeah, have you ever, like — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, if there were a fail, it wouldn’t be funny. (Laughter.) That’s how – I don’t know. That’s a good question. I haven’t thought about that. QUESTION: Was there a moment that one of your kids completely humbled you in front of other parents? MRS RUBIO: No. SECRETARY RUBIO: No. I don’t think so. You kidding? MRS RUBIO: No, our kids never did that. SECRETARY RUBIO: No. They would suffer greatly if (inaudible). MRS RUBIO: (Laughter.) They sure would. It would be a lot of trouble. QUESTION: So what’s the secret to raising happy, well-adjusted, conservative children? MRS RUBIO: You have to talk to them. You have to debate with them. You have to let them tell you what their thoughts are. And usually we would do that when we would sit down and eat, right? I mean, that’s when our conversations would take place. And they would all — SECRETARY RUBIO: My kids talk a lot. MRS RUBIO: Yes, and give us their thoughts. SECRETARY RUBIO: And they like to talk at the same time. So literally, like somebody’s – it happens all the time, and it’s a source of some frustration. MRS RUBIO: It’s true, it’s true. QUESTION: But one child will be speaking, and literally, like, 10 seconds in, a second one will jump on and then start talking at the same time, potentially about a different topic. MRS RUBIO: It’s true. SECRETARY RUBIO: And then a third one will jump in. And so the whole place sounds like – it’s just nuts. And at some point, I’ll have to stop and say hold on, someone was just speaking. There’s not a lot – I don’t know if that even answers your question. These are – we’re just airing grievances now. (Laughter.) But – no, but I think the – this is an interesting question. There are a lot of downsides to being in public service, which I have been basically the entirety of my kids’ lives. That’s the – the time, right? You can’t be in two places at once. So you will miss things. And I think this is true of many careers. But I think the benefit of it, at least, is the kids know that we’ve been doing meaningful things. Like we haven’t been – I haven’t been gone because I’m on a hunting trip every weekend with my friends and not hanging around. They know that what I do is meaningful. And I think as they’ve gotten older, they’ve – whether they – they’ve appreciated that part of it. And so whatever it is they choose to do in their life, I think, will be built on the idea that the purpose of life is to do meaningful things with the time you have and the opportunities that you have. And sometimes meaningful things mean you’ll make money, but sometimes it means you’re not making as much money as someone else but you’re doing things that are really important. And so I hope that that – and the thing people forget about parenting is that the most important thing a parent does is not what you say. It’s what they see you do. MRS RUBIO: A hundred percent. SECRETARY RUBIO: Like for me, the most important lesson I learned from my father – he wasn’t the kind of guy that would sit you down and give you a long talk or whatever. I just saw my dad got up every morning and went to work somewhere. And two weeks out of the year, he didn’t have to work because he got a vacation, but every other day and week of the year, it involved him getting up on time and showing up somewhere and working, even on the days he didn’t want to go, I’m sure. That alone is one of the most important life lessons you’ll learn, and it’s stunning to me how many people don’t learn that. MRS RUBIO: But to add to your question, it really is challenging them, because they do have their thoughts and their views, and allowing them to have them and then respond to them. And that’s what we would do, and it’s worked. My kids are great when it comes to the way – their beliefs, and we’re all pretty aligned, honestly. QUESTION: So now we’re going to move to the game of would you rather. You both answer. Would you rather survive a hurricane with no plumbing and electricity or Disney World during spring break? SECRETARY RUBIO: The hurricane. And Disney World almost at any time at this point. We haven’t been to Disney in probably over a decade — MRS RUBIO: My gosh, for a long time, yeah. SECRETARY RUBIO: But it’s just – not – this is not an anti-Disney thing, but it’s not – not only is it expensive — MRS RUBIO: It’s too expensive. It’s too expensive. SECRETARY RUBIO: — but just in the spring with a lot of people and then it’s hot on top of that, and everyone – I remember the era in Disney where everyone was cheating on the Fast Pass. Remember? QUESTION: On the paper ones? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, so – not only that, but people were – everybody had social anxiety, so they couldn’t make the line. And they were gaming this whole system where everybody was getting – I knew people that were doing this. QUESTION: (Laughter.) Not you. SECRETARY RUBIO: And there was like – you would get a note from a doctor and they’d give you this little pass. (Laughter.) And so all of a sudden you see, like, half the crowd is in the line that doesn’t have to make the wait because they have social anxiety. MRS RUBIO: And it would drive him crazy. (Laughter.) SECRETARY RUBIO: And I’m like, come on, I mean, are we – we’re in the nation of lunatics, if you think about it. And so I think they’ve cracked down on that. But — MRS RUBIO: No, but it’s extremely expensive to take your family nowadays, I think, to Disney World. I mean, it’s a lot. I mean, the food, everything. SECRETARY RUBIO: Now, that said, hurricanes are unpleasant either, but that just tells you how unpleasant the Disney experience can be. MRS RUBIO: Well, you can always leave, right, when there’s a hurricane, because we know ahead of time. SECRETARY RUBIO: Maybe. Yeah, yeah, we can. QUESTION: Would you rather accidentally call a world leader by the wrong name or get caught on camera awkwardly waving at someone who isn’t waving at you? SECRETARY RUBIO: Me? That’s for me, right? MRS RUBIO: I would say the waving. Yeah, I would say the waving. SECRETARY RUBIO: Because she doesn’t talk to – yeah. (Laughter.) So I think – no, no, because, look — MRS RUBIO: Exactly, no, that would be you. SECRETARY RUBIO: Waving at someone who’s not waving at you – neither one is – but you can spin your way out of both of them. Waving at a person who’s not waving at you, you can just say, “What are you talking about?” MRS RUBIO: I would prefer that one. SECRETARY RUBIO: “It was the guy standing right behind him.” But the world leader one is – even if you call them the wrong name, it depends. Like, is it close or is it far? If it’s far, you would say, “Oh, I’m sorry.” I don’t — MRS RUBIO: I would think that one’s more embarrassing. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, that would be more embarrassing. MRS RUBIO: Yeah, yeah. SECRETARY RUBIO: If it was public it would be more embarrassing. QUESTION: Would you rather have control over the thermostat or the remote? MRS RUBIO: Oh, my gosh, we fight for the remote all the time. Because I’ll be watching something and he’ll just come, get the remote, and change it. QUESTION: What’s the ideal temperature? SECRETARY RUBIO: Depends. Daytime or night? MRS RUBIO: Seventy. I would say 70. SECRETARY RUBIO: For – so the science says – you should look this up. MRS RUBIO: Well, sleeping is different than — SECRETARY RUBIO: Sixty-eight degrees is the best sleeping temperature. MRS RUBIO: Right. SECRETARY RUBIO: According to the science, and some interview Tom Brady did. (Laughter.) So it – but during the day you can’t keep it at 68. MRS RUBIO: Seventy. Seventy is the — SECRETARY RUBIO: Seventy, 71, yeah. Depends on the humidity. MRS RUBIO: Seventy – between 70 and 73. SECRETARY RUBIO: Depends on the humidity. MRS RUBIO: Seventy and 73 (inaudible). QUESTION: Would you rather give up Cuban coffee forever or the Miami Dolphins never win another Super Bowl? MRS RUBIO: I would say Cuban coffee. You would – that’s what you would say. SECRETARY RUBIO: I would rather give up Cuban coffee forever? MRS RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: Yeah. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, yeah, but there’s other forms of caffeine. There’s no substitute for a trophy. (Laughter.) QUESTION: Would you rather relive your first year of marriage or relive the years your kids were toddlers? MRS RUBIO: Oh, my gosh, relive my kids are toddlers. SECRETARY RUBIO: But we didn’t really have – like, we didn’t have a first – we had our first child in April of 2001. MRS RUBIO: It just — SECRETARY RUBIO: No, April of 2000. MRS RUBIO: 2000. SECRETARY RUBIO: And we were married in October of ’98. So yeah, there wasn’t a lot of time in between. MRS RUBIO: I would say toddlers, honestly, because it goes by so fast. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. MRS RUBIO: I mean, I can’t look at their pictures or even listen to their voices, which obviously I record, or video without crying, just because it goes by so fast. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: Now we’re in the section where you’re going to only answer with that of another cabinet secretary. SECRETARY RUBIO: Okay. QUESTION: Who do you think is the funniest? SECRETARY RUBIO: In the whole cabinet? QUESTION: Mm-hmm. SECRETARY RUBIO: There are – I think there’s three finalists. I have to say three. So I think the Vice President is funny. Everybody’s got their own style, and I think the Vice President is – can be very funny. I think Bessent in his own way can be very funny, and I mean in his own way – he’s got a different type of presentation. And I think Bobby Kennedy is very funny. Bobby has some of the greatest stories you’ll ever hear. It’s unbelievable, stories that he’ll tell. And you listen to these stories and they’re like, that didn’t really happen. Oh, no, but it did. And I’m not – I mean, I’m talking every day that I sit with him, if you broach a subject, he’ll tell you – the guy has lived an extraordinary life. Like, I was – how is this not a movie? MRS RUBIO: It’s true. It’s true. SECRETARY RUBIO: I mean, it can’t even be a movie. It would have to be a miniseries, because he has so many incredible stories, and many of them are not just funny because that they happened, but they’re just fascinating to me. But he can be funny too. QUESTION: Who’s your best friend in the administration? SECRETARY RUBIO: So the best way to answer that question – I have a lot of people on – so I’ve known J.D. the longest of anybody that’s on there, because he was in the – he was in the Senate with me, but I even knew him before he was a senator and we had interacted on some policy stuff. And then the people I work with the closest on a daily basis, because I just see them all the time, repeatedly, is Pete Hegseth, obviously Scott Bessent we deal with a lot, and John Ratcliffe. That group and that team is constantly interacting with one another as well. So these are the people I’m closest to because we work with the most on an almost daily basis. QUESTION: Who’s always early to meetings? SECRETARY RUBIO: Always early to meetings? I think Ratcliffe is pretty punctual and he shows up. Not that anyone’s late, but he’s usually the first one there. QUESTION: Who’s always late? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, he’s not late. It’s the President. The meeting starts when he gets there, so – (laughter) – but he’s busy. He’s got something going on, so – always, so – but he’s obviously the last to arrive. I don’t think anyone is later per se. I think everyone has gotten to know the President’s scheduling rhythm, and you realize when a meeting is wrapping up, then you head over to the meeting because there’s no point in standing around until he gets there. QUESTION: What’s the funniest thing that’s happened on Air Force One or a government plane that no one’s ever heard about? SECRETARY RUBIO: That I can tell? QUESTION: Yeah, that you can tell. SECRETARY RUBIO: I don’t know if it’s funny. I mean, look, I think there’s been some times on Air Force One – like, I remember coming back from China. I’m not going to say who the person was, but this person was sleeping on one of the couches in the conference room. And for a significant period of this flight, it was debatable whether this person had passed away or not, depending on how they’re sleeping. (Laughter.) I mean, I – I couldn’t see chest movement. I couldn’t see, like, that there – I couldn’t establish a consistent breathing pattern in the individual, but I also didn’t want to wake them up on the one hand or discover a dead body on the other. So we spent a considerable – like 90 minutes sort of debating, should we make a move? Should I call the doc? Should we deal with this? Because it’s embarrassing if you wake him up – oh, I was just sleeping. But if they were dead, like, what do you do? You have a dead body on the plane. Who’s going to – what do you deal with that? I don’t know what the protocol is for it. Luckily, the person was fine and there was no such – so I don’t know if it was funny, but there was a lot of debate about how to approach this particular topic, because there was a lot of noise going on, the lights were on, and this person was not responding to any of the stimulus. And the breathing pattern was difficult. You could see every now and then that there was, like, maybe a breath, but I just – like, I don’t know you sustain life at that pace of respiration. So I don’t know if it was funny, but — MRS RUBIO: Were you watching him the whole time? SECRETARY RUBIO: I kept tabs on it. QUESTION: I kept tabs. SECRETARY RUBIO: Because I just figured, like, I need to account for where I was when this person passed away. MRS RUBIO: Oh, my gosh. SECRETARY RUBIO: Because there’s going to be an investigation and I don’t want – but luckily it all worked out. QUESTION: Of all the cabinet members we’ve interviewed, every single one said you’re the funniest person in the administration. Literally every single one. What’s your best joke, or a joke that you’ve told? SECRETARY RUBIO: So here’s the thing. A lot of the jokes that people consider funny, they’re inside jokes. They wouldn’t make sense for people in their everyday life because they’re things that have happened internally that people view or – and so they – but I don’t know if these are jokes or not jokes, but like, I – I don’t know. I can say this to you. Like, I’m a big Bobby Kennedy fan. I think he’s one of the best people I’ve ever met. Like, the guy truly is pure of heart. So I always – every now and then I’ll tell Bobby, “Bobby, before I met you — MRS RUBIO: He’s great. SECRETARY RUBIO: — I thought you were crazy because that’s what people would say about you.” I said, “Now I believe half your stuff.” (Laughter.) So he thinks that’s really funny. I don’t think that’s, like, a big joke or anything, but I tell him that. And I think Bobby’s one of the most fantastic people I’ve ever met, just such a good, good guy who really is well-intentioned in everything he does and really smart. QUESTION: The Vice President says you have a big sweet tooth. MRS RUBIO: Oh, my gosh. QUESTION: I assume you haven’t adopted RFK’s diet of red meat and fermented vegetables? SECRETARY RUBIO: No. No, this is a crazy diet. This is a – this is a diet that consists of eating sauerkraut and meat. Now, you understand, like, this is not a sustainable thing. Like, you can’t just walk into a — MRS RUBIO: Well, he sustains it because he does it. SECRETARY RUBIO: Can you imagine – he – but he has to travel with coolers of sauerkraut. MRS RUBIO: But he does. He does. SECRETARY RUBIO: I’m not going to travel the world with a cooler full of sauerkraut. It’s ridiculous. I can’t do it. It’s not sustainable for — QUESTION: Are you MAHA? SECRETARY RUBIO: I’m in favor of MAHA. Like, I think people should be healthy. MRS RUBIO: No, he is not. SECRETARY RUBIO: But I think ultimately, at the end — MRS RUBIO: He is completely not. I — QUESTION: What’s he eat? MRS RUBIO: Pop-Tarts. SECRETARY RUBIO: No, I don’t eat Pop-Tarts every day. MRS RUBIO: Okay, you eat sweets. You — SECRETARY RUBIO: The Pop-Tart is one of the great American innovations in the history of the world, if you think about it. It comes in this beautiful foil package. MRS RUBIO: He eats all the things you should not be eating, every single thing. SECRETARY RUBIO: Like what? Like, what do I eat that I should not be eating? MRS RUBIO: Okay. SECRETARY RUBIO: Like other than ice cream. MRS RUBIO: Anything. Anything that – anything that’s sugar, you will take it down. SECRETARY RUBIO: You need carbohydrates to function. (Laughter.) And I would — MRS RUBIO: He will. SECRETARY RUBIO: I did – I — MRS RUBIO: He loves fast food. He loves it all. SECRETARY RUBIO: Okay. I did – at one time maybe four or five years ago, I tried this thing called keto. You’ve heard of this? Okay. QUESTION: Yeah, keto. SECRETARY RUBIO: And you just eat all this protein, and so you go through this massive withdrawal from sugar and carbohydrates for the first 72 hours. It was a near-psychotic event for me. MRS RUBIO: (Laughter.) It’s true. It’s true. SECRETARY RUBIO: Like, if I did this in this job, I would be, “Mr. President, we must bomb Paraguay.” MRS RUBIO: It’s true. SECRETARY RUBIO: And it’s like, “Why?” “I don’t know, I’m just really mad; I haven’t had any sugar.” (Laughter.) So the point is that you can’t – it really is not as – I’m not against this diet. I’m not asking that we ban it. I encourage people to try it. I’m just saying it’s not for everyone. That’s what I’m saying. (Laughter.) QUESTION: I asked the Vice President and Dr. Oz this, so I’m curious: Is the hot dog a sandwich? SECRETARY RUBIO: Is the hot dog a sandwich? QUESTION: Yeah, 57 percent of Americans believe that a hot dog is indeed a sandwich. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, it is a – it’s meat constrained by two pieces of bread, on both sides. MRS RUBIO: Yeah, I would say technically it is. Yeah. SECRETARY RUBIO: So — QUESTION: That’s what Merriam-Webster says, by the way, too. SECRETARY RUBIO: That it is a – that it is a sandwich? MRS RUBIO: Yeah. SECRETARY RUBIO: It is. QUESTION: How do you pick your clothes out in the morning? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I’m colorblind, so I can’t tell, like, certain colors, like green and blue or black and blue or – so I have trouble doing that. So generally speaking, the suits are all dark for the most part. So it’s – I have them ordered. QUESTION: How do you tell which Florsheims go with which outfit? SECRETARY RUBIO: Oh, there’s only – I mean, there’s the one – there’s two Florsheims that we got. One is the tuxedo, and that’s – that I can tell. It’s very shiny. I’m not going to wear that. And then the other one, so it’s the other one. QUESTION: It’s the last question we ask everyone on the pod. SECRETARY RUBIO: Okay. QUESTION: If you could host a dinner party with three people, dead or alive, who’s sitting at the table and what are you eating? SECRETARY RUBIO: A dinner party? QUESTION: Mm-hmm. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, look, as a Christian I would say Jesus, obviously, but that would be a very unique dinner, and I would probably just want to do it one on one. (Laughter.) I don’t want to have a dinner with Jesus and, like, two other people. It’s like, it’d ruin – the whole vibe gets ruined. I want that one on one. So let’s put that one aside for a moment. (Laughter.) I would say I’d be – I’d be fascinated at a – there are various combinations that I could put together. From a political combination, I would say Thatcher, Reagan, and Churchill in the same – it would be really fascinating to hear American president — QUESTION: Interesting you don’t put Jeanette. SECRETARY RUBIO: No, no, you said three people that — MRS RUBIO: Yeah, it is interesting. SECRETARY RUBIO: No, no, but I figure these are people I don’t — MRS RUBIO: I’m alive. She said dead or alive. QUESTION: I said dead or alive. SECRETARY RUBIO: I understand, but that — MRS RUBIO: Yeah, but I am alive. SECRETARY RUBIO: But the context of the question was a dinner that you couldn’t already do. QUESTION: No, I know. I’m giving — SECRETARY RUBIO: Like, this would be a very unique situation. Okay. QUESTION: I’m giving you a hard time. (Laughter.) SECRETARY RUBIO: And then in the realm of, like, athletics, I would love to do a dinner – because I’m a big fan of, like, athletic excellence, because it’s not just a physical ability, it’s the time they put into it. I think Kobe Bryant would have been a fascinating person to talk to; Nick Saban, another high driver in that field and the field of athletics; and then probably the third person that I think would be very fascinating to have in there because of his competitive nature is Magic Johnson. So those three in a room and just pick their brain about what it took and for – to reach the pinnacle of their careers in athletics. Because I think there’s analogies to anything you choose in life, right? In order to be great at something, you have to give up something. You can’t have both. There’s things you can’t do in order to do things you want to do. So it would be fascinating to talk, and two of them are alive; obviously Kobe is not. QUESTION: And what are you eating? SECRETARY RUBIO: Probably sauerkraut and steak. (Laughter.) No, I’m joking. I don’t know. I mean, but something that’s easy to eat so that — QUESTION: What’s the best thing Jeanette makes? SECRETARY RUBIO: Jeanette makes breakfast, fantastic breakfasts. She’s very good at breakfast. That’s her specialty, big time. That said, I mean, I go for the Pop-Tart because it’s much quicker, it’s much more efficient. (Laughter.) But — MRS RUBIO: Exactly. SECRETARY RUBIO: I don’t eat Pop-Tarts every day. This is an exaggeration. If they’re available – like, right now we have no Pop-Tarts at the house, so I’m not eating Pop-Tarts. MRS RUBIO: Because I haven’t bought them. I haven’t purchased them. SECRETARY RUBIO: I don’t go out of my way to buy them, but if they are available, they are very reliable. Because you’re talking about a 30-second process – bang, bang – and then it comes out, it’s ready. So, but she makes excellent breakfast, particularly like scrambled eggs, but she does it in a very unique way. MRS RUBIO: What about dinner? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, but you do that far less – dinner. She’s done it well. I mean, you do. Like, you made — MRS RUBIO: I know. Because you go out — SECRETARY RUBIO: I’m not a big fish-eating person, but she made salmon the other day. It was really good. MRS RUBIO: Yeah, he doesn’t like fish. SECRETARY RUBIO: I don’t like – I mean, it’s not – I’m not anti – like, I’m not against fish. It’s just not my thing. But I’ll eat it. QUESTION: Next headline: “Marco Rubio Is Anti-Fish.” SECRETARY RUBIO: No, no, no, I – fish is good for you, apparently. MRS RUBIO: He is into meat. That’s his thing. QUESTION: Who’s at your dinner party? MRS RUBIO: Who’s at my dinner party? Oh, my gosh. SECRETARY RUBIO: Three people, alive or dead, at your dinner party. MRS RUBIO: Oh, my gosh, I don’t know. I would say people that I loved – my grandmother. SECRETARY RUBIO: Oh, this blew up my answer. (Laughter.) This is terrible. I should have thought of that too. MRS RUBIO: I would say my – my grandmother; of course Christ; and my dad. QUESTION: And what are you making or what are you eating? MRS RUBIO: What am I eating? QUESTION: Yeah. MRS RUBIO: Salmon. (Laughter.) QUESTION: Thank you so much for doing this. SECRETARY RUBIO: Thank you, it was fun. QUESTION: Thanks for watching this episode of the Katie Miller Podcast. Don’t forget, we’re every Tuesday night at 6:00 p.m. See you then. Tags District of Columbia Office of the Spokesperson The Secretary of State

title: State Department Establishes Task Force to End Birth Tourism
text: Home Office of the Spokesperson Press Releases … State Department Establishes Task Force to End Birth Tourism hide State Department Establishes Task Force to End Birth Tourism Fact Sheet Office of the Spokesperson August 12, 2026 Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio’s leadership, the Department of State is using all available tools to defend the integrity of U.S. citizenship, ensure nonimmigrant visas are used only for their lawful and intended purposes, and prevent their exploitation through birth tourism. As President Trump has made clear, citizenship is not a commodity to be acquired through the calculated exploitation of U.S. immigration laws. The Department of State is working closely with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to combat birth tourism and protect the integrity of the U.S. immigration system. New Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force To maximize the success of this comprehensive effort, the State Department has established a Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force. The Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force reviews the activities of visa holders worldwide to identify instances of birth tourism, take action to revoke visas of those who engage in or facilitate it, and dismantle the networks that profit from this abuse. The Task Force addresses the abuse by analyzing and connecting information held across the Department and other federal agencies, including the DHS. Thanks to the coordination of the Task Force, the Department of State is addressing birth tourism on a global scale, examining travel histories of individuals from all around the world in order to end this exploitation and abuse. The Birth Tourism taskforce has taken action by revoking more than 600 visas from foreign nationals across the globe to safeguard our nation from this abuse. The Department generally revokes visas when there are indications of a potential ineligibility. The Secretary has broad discretionary authority to revoke visas – and the Trump Administration is committed to exercising that authority to protect the American people and the integrity of our immigration system. Birth Tourism Has Become a For-Profit Industry Facilitators have turned birth tourism into a lucrative, for-profit industry. These facilitators sometimes market themselves as doulas, midwives, or wellness advocates while openly advertising “birth in the U.S.” services, visa coaching, and hospital arrangements. Some forge medical documents or coach clients to conceal their true travel purpose and avoid paying hospital bills, with online marketing promising clients “automatic citizenship” and “a future without borders.” The facts are clear – birth tourism is a pervasive practice that involves nationals from countries spanning every region of the globe. The Department is taking action to dismantle these networks and hold all participants accountable. Birth Tourism Fraud The work of the Bureau of Consular Affairs Task Force and consular officers at U.S. embassies and consulates around the world is exposing widespread patterns of deception. Foreigners who willfully misrepresent the purpose of their travel or entry into the United States may be permanently ineligible for a U.S. visa or entry to the United States. The Department has uncovered patterns that illustrate the lengths some applicants will go to circumvent our laws in order to secure U.S. citizenship for their children – and potentially for themselves in the future. One couple used a conference and a vacation trip to go shopping as cover stories to give birth to two children in the United States, lying about their travel purpose in two separate visa applications. On the second occasion, the couple concealed that they had a child. The visas have been revoked. In another case, a foreign government official requested a visa to travel on behalf of her government for just one week, but instead stayed three months and gave birth in the United States before departing. The Department revoked the visa. Another traveler applied for a visa to go on vacation in Orlando and instead traveled to Los Angeles and gave birth five days after arrival. The Department revoked the visa. Citizenship is not a commodity to be acquired through calculated exploitation and evasion of the immigration laws. Foreign nationals who abuse the visa system, and those who help them do so, may lose their visa, their access, and their future in the United States. This is only the beginning. Tags Bureau of Consular Affairs Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Office of the Spokesperson The Secretary of State U.S. Visas and Green Cards

title: Department of State Releases 2026 Fiscal Transparency Report
text: Home Office of the Spokesperson Press Releases … Department of State Releases 2026 Fiscal Transparency Report hide Department of State Releases 2026 Fiscal Transparency Report Media Note Office of the Spokesperson August 11, 2026 Today, the Department of State released the 2026 Fiscal Transparency Report (FTR). Fiscal transparency is a critical element of effective public financial management: it helps build market confidence, underpins global economic stability, and levels the playing field for U.S. firms. It fosters greater government accountability by providing a window into government budgets and spending. Congress mandated annual reviews of fiscal transparency to help ensure the appropriate use of U.S. taxpayer funds related to foreign assistance. In this year’s report, Department officials found that 73 of 139 governments and one entity assessed met the minimum fiscal transparency requirements. Sixty-seven did not meet the minimum fiscal transparency requirements, but of those 14 made significant progress toward meeting the minimum fiscal transparency requirements. The report describes the minimum fiscal transparency requirements and reviews the governments and entity assessed, most of which were identified as recipients of U.S. assistance in the 2014 Fiscal Transparency Report. The Department evaluated the public availability, completeness, and reliability of budget documents, as well as the transparency of processes for awarding government contracts and licenses and public procurement contracts. The Fiscal Transparency Report helps create competitive business conditions for U.S. companies abroad by improving public financial management to reduce the risk of corruption and unfair practices in international markets, promoting stronger industry standards to improve market access, reducing the risk of financial crimes, and requiring debt data disclosure to counter predatory lending. You can find the Fiscal Transparency Report , as well as information about the Fiscal Transparency Innovation Fund , on our website. For further information, please contact the Bureau of Economic, Energy and Business Affairs’ Fiscal Transparency team at fiscaltransparency@state.gov . Tags Bureau of Economic, Energy, and Business Affairs Economy and Trade Policy Finance and Investments Office of the Spokesperson Reports

title: Release of Robert Gilman
text: Home Office of the Spokesperson Press Releases … Release of Robert Gilman hide Release of Robert Gilman Press Statement Marco Rubio, Secretary of State August 11, 2026 Today, after more than four years of detention in Russia, Robert Gilman is on his way home to be reunited with his family. Mr. Gilman joins over 100 Americans whom President Trump has freed during his second term in office. We thank Russia for working with Special Envoy Steve Witkoff to release Mr. Gilman and allowing him to receive the necessary medical treatment here in the United States. While we appreciate this positive step, we are still seeking the immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans, including wrongful detainee Stephen Hubbard. The President will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home.
